questions.topic: The number of marks on the printed dynamic scale
questions.learningObjective: count the marks on the main dynamic scale and the steps between them
questions.stem: The printed dynamic scale used in 4/4, common time, in c major runs through seven marks, from the softest to the loudest: pianississimo, piano, mezzo piano, mezzo forte, forte, fortissimo and fortississimo. How many separate steps separate the softest mark from the loudest one?
questions.explanation: A run of seven marks has six gaps between them, and the count of steps is one less than the count of marks, which is the ordinary off-by-one in any ranked list. Listing them in order makes the structure plain: pianississimo to piano is one, piano to mezzo piano is two, mezzo piano to mezzo forte is three, mezzo forte to forte is four, forte to fortissimo is five, and fortissimo to fortississimo is six. Two features of the list are worth noticing and both follow from what the marks name. The first is that the middle two marks are the same two words with the other adjective, so mezzo piano and mezzo forte are the same middle term with the direction reversed, which is why a scale of seven still has a single centre rather than two. The second is that a crescendo from piano to forte covers three steps while a diminuendo from forte to piano covers the same three, so the two markings are mirror images in both size and direction. The trap is 7, which counts the marks rather than the intervals between them, and the trap of 8 would come from assuming a mark at each end beyond the extremes.
questions.hint: Count the gaps between the seven marks, not the marks themselves.

questions.topic: What the marking forte instructs
questions.learningObjective: state what a printed dynamic mark instructs a player to do
questions.stem: The mark forte is printed at the start of a bar in 4/4, common time, in c major, and that bar holds a written C5 quarter note, a written E5 quarter note and a written G5 quarter note. What does the mark instruct, and what does it leave undecided?

options.text: Forte instructs the player to make the three notes louder than the previous bar, and it leaves the exact loudness undecided, because a mark compares a passage with what came before it
options.misconception: reads a dynamic mark as an instruction to increase rather than to set a level

options.text: Forte instructs a loud dynamic level for the passage, and it leaves the exact loudness undecided, because a mark is a relative instruction within the piece rather than a measured volume
Forte instructs a loud dynamic level and fixes it exactly, because the mark corresponds to a measured number of decibels on a sound level meter
options.misconception: believes a printed dynamic carries an absolute decibel value

options.text: Forte instructs the player to double the speed of the three notes and leave the loudness as written elsewhere in the part
options.misconception: confuses a dynamic mark with a tempo marking

questions.explanation: A dynamic mark sets a level rather than a change, which is the distinction that trips most readers. Forte is a strong level, and a player taking it at face value plays the three notes loudly and continues to play them at that level until another mark moves the level, so the passage has one sustained quality rather than a shape. What the mark does not do is specify a measured loudness: a sound level meter would show a wide range of intensities for performances that all sound convincingly forte, because the mark is calibrated by comparison within the music and by the acoustic of the hall, neither of which is written on the page. The trap in the first option is the common misreading that a dynamic is a change rather than a state, and that reading produces the same mistake in a diminuendo, which would then be a fall rather than a quiet level. The trap in the third option confuses two different families of mark: dynamics concern loudness and tempo markings concern speed, and the two are independent, so a part can be marked forte and remain at one speed throughout.
questions.hint: Separate a level from a change of level, and separate loudness from speed.

questions.topic: What the marking crescendo instructs
questions.learningObjective: state what a crescendo mark instructs and how far it moves
questions.stem: A crescendo wedge is printed under a bar in 4/4, common time, in c major, and that bar holds a written C5 half note followed by a written E5 half note. What does the mark instruct across the bar, and where does the increase stop?

options.text: The mark instructs a gradual increase of loudness from the first note to the last, and the increase stops where the next dynamic mark or the end of the passage says it does, not at the bar line
The mark instructs an increase of speed across the bar, and the increase stops at the bar line because the marking is printed under that bar alone
options.misconception: treats a crescendo as a tempo change bounded by the bar

options.text: The mark instructs a sudden increase on the first note of the bar, and the increase continues until a diminuendo is printed
options.misconception: reads a gradual hairpin as an immediate accent

options.text: The mark instructs the two notes to be played with a louder second note and a softer first, so the bar ends where the increase began
options.misconception: reverses the direction of a crescendo

questions.explanation: A crescendo is a hairpin, an opening pair of lines, and it asks for a gradual rise in loudness across whatever span it covers. The word that matters is gradual, because the marking's whole effect depends on the rise being continuous: a sudden jump at the first note would be an accent, not a crescendo, and the third option's reversed reading would be a diminuendo. The extent is decided by the next mark rather than by the bar, which is why the second option's bar-line boundary is wrong: a composer who wants the hairpin to stop mid-bar can either close it there or place the next dynamic letter at the change, and a hairpin running under a bar line is completely normal. A useful check is the printed form itself, since an opening wedge is a crescendo and a closing wedge is a diminuendo, so a reader can confirm the direction from the shape of the sign without knowing either word. The dynamics and the rhythm stay independent throughout, which is why the two half notes keep their written two beats each however the loudness behaves.
questions.hint: A crescendo is an opening wedge and covers the span up to the next mark, not up to the bar line.

questions.topic: The span of a crescendo measured in scale steps
questions.learningObjective: measure a dynamic change in steps of the printed scale
questions.stem: Starting at piano and rising through a passage in 4/4, common time, in c major, a crescendo is asked to reach a marked level. On the printed scale of pianississimo, piano, mezzo piano, mezzo forte, forte, fortissimo and fortississimo, how many steps does a rise from piano to forte cover?
questions.explanation: The passage is piano to forte, and reading the scale in order gives piano, mezzo piano, mezzo forte, forte, which is three steps: piano up to mezzo piano is one, mezzo piano up to mezzo forte is two, and mezzo forte up to forte is three. The same three steps measure a diminuendo from forte back to piano, because the scale is symmetric about its two middle marks, so a rise and a fall of equal extent are the same distance. The check against the seven marks confirms the arithmetic: piano is the second mark from the soft end and forte is the fifth, and five minus two is three. The practical point is that a composer writing a hairpin decides how large a change it should be by choosing marks that are a comfortable distance apart on this scale, and a change of one step is a light touch while a change of four or more is a large one that most players will approach over several bars. The trap is 2, which comes from reading the pair of middle terms as one step, and 4, which comes from counting the three intermediate marks along with the three gaps.
questions.hint: Number the marks from the soft end and subtract the two positions.

questions.topic: The direction a hairpin points
questions.learningObjective: read the direction of a hairpin from its shape
questions.stem: A hairpin is printed under a written G4 half note in 4/4, common time, in c major, with its two lines meeting at the left and opening to the right. What does the sign instruct, and how does its shape differ from the opposite mark?

options.text: The sign instructs a diminuendo, and an opening wedge grows louder to the right while a diminuendo opens to the left
options.misconception: reverses which wedge shape means crescendo

options.text: The sign instructs a crescendo, and a diminuendo is drawn as a longer version of the same opening wedge with no change of shape
options.misconception: believes both hairpins share one shape

options.text: The sign instructs a general increase in loudness for the whole movement, and its shape records the length of the increase rather than its direction
options.misconception: reads a hairpin as a movement-wide instruction

options.text: The sign instructs a crescendo, and an opening wedge grows louder to the right, while a diminuendo is drawn as a closing wedge whose lines meet at the right

questions.explanation: A hairpin is a pair of straight lines whose spacing at any point records the loudness at that point, and the direction of opening is the direction of increase. Lines that meet at the left and spread to the right show a rise, which is a crescendo, and lines that spread at the left and meet at the right show a fall, which is a diminuendo. The shape is therefore a graph of the volume, and a player reading a wedge that widens across a bar is being told to widen the sound across that bar. This is also why a hairpin can be graded in extent: a wedge that opens by a small amount asks for a small change, and one that opens widely across a whole page asks for a large one, which is a finer control than the seven discrete letter marks can give. The trap in the third option misreads a local mark as a global one, and the trap in the first reverses the shapes, which is the single most common error in reading a hairpin and one that a glance at the geometry catches immediately.
questions.hint: Look at which end of the wedge is narrow: the narrow end is where the loudness starts.

questions.topic: What the marking staccato instructs
questions.learningObjective: state what a staccato dot does to a note
questions.stem: A staccato dot is printed above the note head of a written C5 quarter note in 4/4, common time, in c major. What does the dot instruct, and what does it leave unchanged?

options.text: The dot instructs the note to be played twice as fast as written, so the pitch stays C5 but the duration is halved
options.misconception: treats staccato as a change of note value rather than of note length in time

options.text: The dot instructs the note to be played more loudly than written, so the pitch and the duration are both unchanged
options.misconception: confuses an articulation mark with a dynamic mark

options.text: The dot instructs the note to be released early, so it occupies less than its written value and the remainder is added to the following silence, while the pitch C5 is unchanged
The dot instructs the note to be slurred into the following note, so the written quarter note merges with the next written value
options.misconception: treats staccato as a legato mark

questions.explanation: A staccato dot is an articulation mark, and articulation marks concern how a note is joined to its neighbours, not how loud it is or what pitch it has. The dot asks for separation: the player releases the note before its written time is up and lets the remainder of that time be silence, so a staccato quarter note sounds for roughly a third of a beat and is followed by a silence of the other two thirds. The two consequences worth stating are that the sounding length is shorter while the notated grid is unchanged, so a bar still contains four beats' worth of positions however short each note sounds, and that the note is detached from what follows rather than connected to it. The trap in the first option is the confusion that makes staccato sound like a rhythmic change: the note's written value has not altered, and the bar has not got shorter, so a player counting beats in a dotted passage still counts the same numbers. The trap in the third option reverses the mark, since a slur joins and a dot separates.
questions.hint: A staccato dot shortens the sounding note and leaves the written value and the pitch alone.

questions.topic: What the marking tenuto instructs
questions.learningObjective: state what a tenuto line instructs and how it differs from staccato
questions.stem: A short horizontal line is printed above the note head of a written G4 quarter note in 4/4, common time, in c major. What does that mark instruct, and how does its effect contrast with a staccato dot on the same note?

options.text: The line is a tenuto mark and it instructs the note to fill its full written value, which is the same as what a staccato dot asks for on that note
options.misconception: believes a tenuto line and a staccato dot agree

options.text: The line is tenuto, and it instructs the note to fill its full written value, which is the opposite of the staccato dot that shortens the note and separates it from what follows
The line instructs the note to be held for twice its written value, and the staccato dot instructs the same doubling in the opposite direction
options.misconception: reads a tenuto line as a doubling rather than a full value

options.text: The line is a breath mark and it instructs the player to breathe at that point, which is what a staccato dot also does when it follows a rest
options.misconception: confuses a tenuto line with a breath mark

questions.explanation: Tenuto comes from the Italian tenere, to hold, and the sign asks for the note to occupy its whole written value and to be given its full weight. That makes it the natural partner to a staccato dot and the clearest way to state the contrast: on the same written quarter note, tenuto asks for the full beat and staccato asks for about a third of it, so the two marks span the whole range of what an unmeasured note length can be. The placement of the mark helps too, since a tenuto line is written above or below the note head where a staccato dot is written beside it, and neither of those is a breath mark, which is a comma placed in the space above the staff and is the one member of this family that is not attached to a note. The trap in the second option is a common over-reading, because tenuto means full value and not double value, and a composer who wants twice the written time writes a fermata instead.
questions.hint: Tenuto means hold the full value, which is the opposite instruction to a staccato dot.

questions.topic: The fraction a staccato note keeps of its written value
questions.learningObjective: compute the sounding length of a staccato note from the printed value
questions.stem: A written E4 quarter note in 4/4, common time, in c major carries a staccato dot, and the convention is that a staccato note sounds for about one third of its written value. A quarter note is one beat, so how many beats does that staccato quarter note sound for, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: One third of one beat is 0.3333 beats, which rounds to 0.33 beats, and the remaining two thirds of the beat, about 0.67 beats, is silence. The check is that the two parts must add to the whole: 0.33 plus 0.67 is 1.00, the full written value, which is the invariant that makes a staccato passage a matter of articulation rather than of rhythm. The practical significance is in the texture: a bar of staccato notes at one beat each is much lighter in sound than the same bar legato, and it is lighter not because the notes are lower or shorter in the score but because the gaps between them let each note decay, and decay is what a listener hears as lightness. The figure is a convention rather than a measurement, which is why the marking is written as a dot and not as a note value, and which is why a player is free to make the staccato shorter in a slow passage and longer in a fast one. The trap is 0.5, which is the value a staccatissimo or a portato would approach, and 1.0, which is tenuto.
questions.hint: One third of one beat, and the rest of the beat is silence.

questions.topic: What the marking marcato instructs
questions.learningObjective: state what a marcato mark instructs and how strongly it is applied
questions.stem: A small upright wedge, the sign sometimes called marcato, is printed above the note head of a written G4 quarter note in 4/4, common time, in c major. What does the mark instruct, and where does its force sit on the scale of articulations?

options.text: The mark instructs the note to be played markedly, with extra weight and a slight emphasis above the ordinary level, and it sits above a plain note but below the strongest marking a composer can apply
The mark instructs the note to be played as loudly as possible, since the wedge points upward and an upward sign always means a maximum dynamic
options.misconception: reads a marcato wedge as a maximum dynamic

options.text: The mark instructs the note to be shortened as much as a staccato dot shortens it, since both marks sit close to the note head
options.misconception: reads a marcato wedge as a shortening mark

options.text: The mark instructs the player to rest on the note for its full value, since the wedge is a vertical version of the tenuto line
options.misconception: reads a marcato wedge as a tenuto line

questions.explanation: Marcato is an articulation mark that asks for a note to stand out from its neighbours, and it combines a little extra weight with a slight accent rather than acting only on loudness or only on length. That combination is what makes it hard to place on a single scale, and the honest description is that it sits between an ordinary note and the most forceful marking available: a composer who wants more reaches for sforzando or for a written accent with a dynamic letter, and a marcato is a shade less than either. Its position on the page is a useful check, because it is written above or below the note head as a small upright wedge, distinct from the horizontal line of tenuto and from the dot of staccato, so a reader can identify it from its shape without knowing the word. The trap in the first option is the geometric mistake of reading a point as a level: a wedge that points upward marks emphasis, not volume, and a composer who wants volume writes a letter. The trap in the third is a shape confusion with tenuto, which is a line rather than a wedge and which lengthens rather than emphasises.
questions.hint: A marcato wedge asks for extra weight and a slight accent, not a maximum dynamic.

questions.topic: The fraction a staccatissimo note keeps of its written value
questions.learningObjective: compute the sounding length of the shortest staccato mark
questions.stem: The staccatissimo wedge is printed on a written D5 eighth note in 4/4, common time, in c major, and the convention is that such a note sounds for about one sixteenth of its written value. An eighth note is half a beat, so how many beats does that note sound for, to three decimal places?
questions.explanation: One sixteenth of half a beat is half divided by sixteen, which is 0.03125 beats, and to three decimal places that is 0.031. The arithmetic is worth doing in the stated order, because dividing a beat by sixteen and then by two gives the same answer and confirms the reading: 1 divided by 16 is 0.0625, and 0.0625 divided by 2 is 0.03125. The gap that results is large, about 0.47 of a beat of silence, which is what makes staccatissimo the lightest of the dot family and what makes it a marking for a quick, dry, thrown note rather than for a sustained one. The comparison with the staccato dot is the useful part, since a staccato eighth note would sound a third of half a beat, about 0.167 beats, so staccatissimo is roughly five times shorter than staccato on the same note. Nothing about the pitch changes, so D5 remains D5, and nothing about the bar changes, so the bar still contains four beats of notated time. The trap is 0.0625, which is the fraction of a whole beat rather than of the written half beat, and 0.125, which is one eighth.
questions.hint: Half a beat divided by sixteen, and note that the fraction is of the written value rather than of a whole beat.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that shortens a note for staccato
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that divides a written duration by three
questions.stem: Trace the rule sounded(written), which returns the sounding length in beats of a note marked staccato: sounded(written) = return written / 3. Apply it to a bar in 4/4, common time, in c major holding a written C5 quarter note, a written E5 eighth note and a written G5 eighth note, all three marked staccato. What three sounding lengths does the rule return?

options.text: 1 beat, then 0.5 beats, then 0.5 beats, since the rule returns the written duration unchanged and the staccato dot is a marking without effect on length
options.misconception: believes an articulation mark leaves the sounding length alone

options.text: 0.5 beats, then 0.25 beats, then 0.25 beats, since the rule halves each written duration rather than dividing it by three
options.misconception: divides by two instead of by three

options.text: 0.333 beats, then 0.167 beats, then 0.167 beats, but the bar then contains only 0.667 beats, so the bar is a third shorter as well
options.misconception: shortens the bar as well as the notes

options.text: 0.333 beats, then 0.167 beats, then 0.167 beats, since the three written values are 1, 0.5 and 0.5 beats and each is divided by three

questions.explanation: Three divisions and one conversion of units, and the unit has to be fixed first. A quarter note is one beat, an eighth note is half a beat, and a dotted quarter would be one and a half beats, so the written values here are 1, 0.5 and 0.5. Dividing each by three gives 0.3333, 0.1667 and 0.1667 beats, which is the answer. The third option is the one worth taking seriously and then rejecting, because the question of whether the bar gets shorter is exactly the point: it does not. The rule changes how long each note sounds and leaves the notated grid alone, so the bar still holds four beats of written time with three positions in it, and the player counts the same numbers whether the notes are staccato or legato. That is the practical definition of articulation, which is a way of playing written durations rather than a way of rewriting them. The trap in the second option is the arithmetic of a halving, which is what a staccatissimo approaches and is close enough to feel familiar.
questions.hint: Convert each written note to beats first, then divide each by three.

questions.topic: What a fermata instructs and what it does not
questions.learningObjective: state the scope and limits of a fermata
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in c major places a fermata, an arc with a dot beneath it, above a written G4 half note at the end of a phrase. What does the sign instruct, and what does it leave to the performer?

options.text: The sign instructs the player to hold the note for twice its written value, and it leaves the tempo unchanged so the bar stays exactly four beats long
options.misconception: reads a fermata as a fixed doubling that also fixes the tempo

options.text: The sign instructs the player to breathe before the note, and it leaves the sounding length of the note equal to its written value
options.misconception: confuses a fermata with a breath mark

options.text: The sign instructs the player to hold the note beyond its written value, and it leaves the length of the hold entirely to the performer, since no printed mark fixes a duration in seconds
The sign instructs the player to play the note louder than marked, and it leaves the written value of the note unchanged
options.misconception: reads a fermata as a dynamic mark

questions.explanation: A fermata asks for a hold, and the word hold is the whole of its meaning: the note is sustained past the point where the bar would have moved on, at the performer's discretion, and the ensemble then re-enters together. What a fermata never does is fix a length. There is no printed duration in seconds, and a fermata over a single note in a slow movement may last a beat while the same mark in a fast movement may last less, because the mark is an instruction about emphasis and time rather than an amount of time. That is the practical reason a conductor decides the length and the players watch, and the reason the mark appears in scores of widely different tempos without any conversion factor attached. The trap in the first option is the attempt to make the fermata quantitative, and its second half is worse still, because holding a note past its written value necessarily delays the bar. The trap in the second confuses the fermata with the breath mark, which is a comma above the staff placed in a gap rather than an arc over a note.
questions.hint: A fermata asks for a hold and fixes no length of time.

questions.topic: The sign for a down-bow
questions.learningObjective: identify the printed sign for a down-bow
questions.stem: A violin part in 4/4, common time, in d major prints a marking above a written D4 quarter note instructing the player how to set the bow on the string. What does the sign for a down-bow look like, and what does it ask the player to do?

options.text: It is drawn as a closed circle and it asks the player to set the bow at the middle of the string and draw it towards the tip
options.misconception: confuses the down-bow sign with a harmonic circle

options.text: It is drawn as a squared bracket open at the bottom, a shape like a squared pi, and it asks the player to set the bow on the string and draw it towards the frog, from the tip towards the hand
It is drawn as a squared bracket open at the bottom and it asks the player to draw the bow away from the hand, from the frog towards the tip
options.misconception: reverses the direction the down-bow travels

options.text: It is drawn as a short vertical line and it asks the player to lift the bow from the string and set it down again without drawing
options.misconception: treats the down-bow sign as a lift rather than a stroke

questions.explanation: The two bowing signs are mirror images, and once the shape is fixed the direction follows. A down-bow is drawn as a squared bracket whose closed side is at the bottom, which looks like a squared pi or a table, and an up-bow is the same shape turned over with the closed side at the top, which looks like a squared U. The down-bow moves the bow from the tip towards the frog, that is towards the player's hand, and the up-bow reverses that. The reason the distinction matters at all is timbral rather than merely notational, because the bow's weight and the string's motion are greatest near the frog and least near the tip, so the same stroke sounds different in the two directions and composers use the marks to control where in the stroke a passage sits. The trap in the first option is a real and different sign, since a small circle above or below a note asks for a harmonic rather than for a bow stroke, and the trap in the second reverses the direction while keeping the right shape.
questions.hint: The down-bow sign is a squared bracket closed at the bottom, and it draws the bow towards the hand.

questions.topic: The sign for an up-bow
questions.learningObjective: identify the printed sign for an up-bow
questions.stem: A cello part in 4/4, common time, in d major prints a bowing marking above a written A3 quarter note asking for the stroke that returns the bow to the tip. What does that sign look like, and how does it differ in shape from the sign for the other stroke?

options.text: It is drawn as a squared bracket closed at the top, a squared U, and it is the vertical mirror image of the down-bow sign, which is closed at the bottom
It is drawn as a squared bracket closed at the bottom, and it differs from the down-bow sign only in being printed below the note rather than above it
options.misconception: keeps the down-bow shape and moves it instead of turning it over

options.text: It is drawn as a short vertical line, and it differs from the down-bow sign in having no closed side at all
options.misconception: describes a lift mark as the up-bow sign

options.text: It is drawn as an arc with a dot beneath it, and it differs from the down-bow sign in suspending the bow before it moves
options.misconception: confuses the up-bow sign with a fermata

questions.explanation: The up-bow and down-bow signs differ only in which end of the bracket is closed, and that is enough to tell them apart at a glance because the two are exact vertical reflections of one another. Closed at the top is the up-bow, which travels from the frog towards the tip, and closed at the bottom is the down-bow, which travels the other way. The practical reason a part needs them is bow distribution: a passage of even quavers has to be divided so that the bow reverses at sensible points, and a written stroke alternates automatically in the player's head, whereas leaving it out invites an uneven stroke in a hurry. The trap in the first option is the most natural error, because a reader who knows the down-bow sign and sees the instruction reversed tends to assume only the position on the page has changed, when in fact the shape itself is what carries the meaning. The trap in the third confuses a bowing mark with a fermata, which is an arc with a dot and which suspends the note rather than moving the bow.
questions.hint: The up-bow sign is the down-bow sign turned upside down: closed at the top.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that alternates bow directions
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that alternates a two-valued flag across a bar
questions.stem: Trace the rule stroke(i), which returns the bowing mark for the ith note of a bar, counting i from 1: stroke(i) = return "down" if i is odd, and "up" if i is even. Apply it to a bar in 4/4, common time, in d major holding four written quarter notes, D4, F#4, A4 and D5. What four bowing marks does the rule return?

options.text: down, down, up, up, since the rule groups the notes in pairs and reverses only at the start of each pair
options.misconception: reverses every second note instead of every note

options.text: up, down, up, down, since the rule counts from 0 rather than from 1 and therefore starts with the even case
options.misconception: starts the alternation on the up-bow

options.text: down, up, down, up, but the rule must restart at each bar line, so the third note of the bar is played with an up-bow
options.misconception: believes the alternation resets at the bar line

options.text: down, up, down, up, since 1 and 3 are odd and 2 and 4 are even, so the bow alternates at every note across the bar

questions.explanation: Four applications of the rule and the parity test settles each one. With i counting from 1, the values are 1, 2, 3 and 4, and odd values give a down-bow while even values give an up-bow, so the sequence is down, up, down, up. That the first note is a down-bow is a convention rather than a law, and it is the source of the second distractor: a rule written to count from 0 would begin with the even case and produce up, down, up, down, which is a perfectly usable bowing and is simply not what this rule says. The third distractor raises a real question about bar lines, and the honest answer is that the rule as stated has no bar-line term, so it does not restart; whether a player in fact begins each new bar on a down-bow is a separate habit that a composer would have to ask for with an explicit mark. In a passage of even note values, alternating at every note is the natural default because it distributes the bow evenly and keeps the tone consistent.
questions.hint: Count the notes from 1 and test each index for odd or even.

questions.topic: Why players take a breath where a breath mark is printed
questions.learningObjective: explain the function of a printed breath mark
questions.stem: A small comma is printed above the staff in the gap between a written G4 quarter note and a written D5 quarter note of a vocal part in 4/4, common time, in g major. Why is the mark placed there rather than over a note, and what does it instruct?

options.text: The mark is placed in a gap because it belongs to the following note, and it instructs the singer to begin that note with an audible accent
options.misconception: makes a breath mark an accent on the next note

options.text: The mark is placed in a gap because it lengthens the silence, and it instructs the singer to hold the breath for a written number of beats
options.misconception: reads a breath mark as a fermata in a gap

options.text: The mark is placed in a gap because it belongs to no note, and it instructs the singer to take a breath in that silence, which is why it is only ever printed where the score leaves room for one
The mark is placed in a gap because breath marks are never written over notes, and it instructs the singer to inhale audibly so the audience can hear the phrase divide
options.misconception: believes the breath is meant to be audible

questions.explanation: A breath mark is a comma, and a comma is a mark of punctuation rather than of duration, which is why it belongs to the space between two notes and never sits over a note head. Its instruction is simple and functional: take a breath in the silence there. That means the score must have left a silence to breathe in, and a composer who wants a breath at a point where the notes run on has to either shorten a value or place the mark at the natural gap, which is why breath marks cluster at phrase ends and where a rest or a long note already provides the room. The convention that the breath is silent follows from the purpose, since an audible inhale would announce the phrasing to the audience instead of helping the singer phrase it, and singers are trained to breathe where it will not be heard. The trap in the third option is the one a beginner sometimes meets in choral rehearsals, where the instruction is given aloud precisely so that everyone breathes together and nobody is left unprepared. The trap in the second confuses a mark that opens a gap with one that measures a hold.
questions.hint: A breath mark is a comma in a gap, and the breath is taken silently during the silence.

questions.topic: What a phrasing slur does across a bar line
questions.learningObjective: explain what a phrase slur asks for across a bar line
questions.stem: A single slur runs from a written E4 quarter note in bar one to a written C5 half note in bar two of a piano part in 4/4, common time, in c major. What does the slur ask the player to do, and why must a slur be told apart from a tie?

options.text: The slur asks the player to hold the E4 for the whole of bar two as well, and it is told from a tie because a tie covers different pitches while a slur covers the same pitch
options.misconception: reverses which mark joins equal pitches

options.text: The slur asks the player to play the covered notes legato, in one connected gesture across the bar line, and it is told from a tie because a tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer note while a slur joins different pitches
The slur asks the player to play the notes at a uniform dynamic level, and it is told from a tie because a tie changes loudness while a slur changes nothing
options.misconception: reads a slur as a dynamic marking

options.text: The slur asks the player to breathe before the C5, and it is told from a tie because a slur marks a phrase end while a tie marks a phrase continuation
options.misconception: confuses a slur with a breath mark

questions.explanation: A slur is an instruction about connection, and it can span any number of notes of any pitches within one gesture, including across a bar line, which is exactly what the two notes here require. Its neighbour is the tie, and the two are distinguished by pitch: a tie joins two notes of the same pitch into a single longer sound, so a tied E4 quarter and E4 half becomes one E4 of three beats, whereas a slur joining E4 to C5 is a legato instruction about two different notes and produces two sounds. The visual difference follows the same logic, since a tie is a short curved line joining two note heads of identical pitch and a slur is a longer curve whose ends sit near the note heads it covers. The trap in the first option is the reversal, and it is worth stating plainly because a tie and a slur are the classic pair of confusions in the subject: a tie changes the sounding length of one note and a slur changes the articulation between notes, and neither of them changes pitch or dynamic.
questions.hint: A tie joins equal pitches into one longer note; a slur asks for legato between different pitches.

questions.topic: Reading a table of expression marks
questions.learningObjective: extract from a table which markings change duration and which do not
questions.stem: A table lists six markings with the effect each asks for: forte, which asks for a loud level; crescendo, which asks for a gradual increase; tenuto, which asks for the full written value; staccato, which asks for a short separated note; marcato, which asks for extra weight; and fermata, which asks for a hold beyond the written value. Which three of the six change the sounding length of a note, and which three do not?

options.text: Tenuto, staccato and fermata change the sounding length, while forte, crescendo and marcato leave the length alone and concern loudness or emphasis instead
Forte, crescendo and marcato change the sounding length, while tenuto, staccato and fermata leave the length alone
options.misconception: reverses which family of marks concerns length

options.text: All six change the sounding length, since every expressive mark alters how long a note is heard as well as how loud it is
options.misconception: believes every expression mark affects duration

options.text: Only staccato and fermata change the sounding length, because tenuto asks only for emphasis and does not concern the note full stop
options.misconception: excludes tenuto from the marks that concern length

questions.explanation: The table can be sorted on one criterion: does the mark talk about time or about intensity. Tenuto, staccato and fermata all name a length, so they change how long the note is heard: tenuto to the full written value, staccato to a fraction of it, fermata beyond it. Forte, crescendo and marcato all name a level or a weight, so they leave the length alone and act on how the note sounds while it is sounding. The cross-check is to ask of each mark what it would still mean in a performance at a single steady dynamic, and a forte or a crescendo would vanish entirely while a staccato or a fermata would still be audible, which confirms the split. The trap in the first option is the reversal, and it is easy to fall into because a crescendo and a fermata are both drawn as a widening or a hold and look similar in shape, which is a reminder that shape does not decide meaning here. The trap in the third is the interesting near-miss, because tenuto does add emphasis as well as length, but the length is still part of what it asks for, and a note played to its full value with no weight is not what the mark means.
questions.hint: Sort the six marks by whether they name a length or a level.

questions.topic: Distinguishing accent marks that sit above and below the staff
questions.learningObjective: tell an accent mark from the hairpin and from staccato
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in c major carries several marks above and below its note heads. Which of the following statements about them is true? Select every statement that holds.

options.text: A single written accent, a small wedge opening downwards placed above the note head, asks for that one note to be played with extra weight, and it does not ask for any change of loudness over time
A hairpin, which is a wedge whose two lines meet at one end, asks for a continuous change of loudness across the span it covers, and its direction is read from which end the lines meet at
A single written accent and a hairpin ask for the same thing, since both are wedges and a wedge always means an increase in loudness
options.misconception: treats a single accent as a hairpin

options.text: A staccato dot and a hairpin both change the sounding length of a note, since both sit close to the note head and shorten it
options.misconception: gives a hairpin a duration effect

questions.explanation: Two of the four statements hold and they describe different things. A single accent, printed as a small wedge that opens downwards above the note head, is a point instruction: it asks for that one note to carry extra weight and to stand out from its neighbours, and nothing about the notes around it changes. A hairpin is also a wedge, but its two lines meet at one end and open at the other, which makes it a continuous instruction across a span, and the direction follows from the geometry rather than from any word. The two false statements both come from reading shape as meaning. The first treats every wedge alike and so misses that a single accent has no width in time while a hairpin does, and the second mistakes a hairpin for a note-length mark, which is a confusion with the dot family: a dot shortens one note and a hairpin alters the level of a passage without altering any note's length. The third swaps the two roles and is the most useful correction, since the accent is the emphatic single-note mark and the hairpin is the mark that never emphasises a single note in isolation.
questions.hint: A single accent is a point about one note; a hairpin is a slope across a span.

questions.topic: The dynamics a passage inherits from the mark before it
questions.learningObjective: track which printed dynamic governs which notes in a part
questions.stem: Marks are distributed across three bars of a part in 4/4, common time, in c major as follows. Bar one carries forte and holds a written C5 quarter note, a written E5 quarter note and a written G5 half note. Bar two carries a crescendo and holds a written C5 half note and a written G5 half note. Bar three carries no dynamic mark at all and holds a written E5 half note and a written G4 half note. Which printed level governs the two notes of bar three, and how many steps of the printed dynamic scale separate the opening forte from the level the crescendo reaches?

options.text: The notes of bar three are governed by the crescendo of bar two, because a hairpin sets a level for the passage that follows it, and the crescendo reaches fortissimo, one step above forte
options.misconception: treats a hairpin as a level

options.text: The notes of bar three are governed by the forte of bar one, because a dynamic letter holds until another replaces it, and the crescendo reaches fortississimo, two steps above forte
options.misconception: keeps the right level but miscounts the scale steps

options.text: The notes of bar three carry no dynamic at all, because a mark applies only to the bar in which it is printed and does not carry over
options.misconception: believes a dynamic expires at the bar line

options.text: The notes of bar three are governed by the forte of bar one, because a dynamic letter holds until another one replaces it and a hairpin is a change rather than a level, and the crescendo reaches fortissimo, one step above forte

questions.explanation: Two separate readings are needed here, and the first is about what persists. A letter mark such as forte sets a level that holds until another letter replaces it, so it governs the whole of bar three, since bar three contains no letter. A hairpin is not a letter and does not set a level, which is why the crescendo of bar two cannot be the governing mark even though it is the most recent instruction of any kind. The second reading is the count, and the printed scale gives it: from forte, one step up is fortissimo, and a crescendo that starts at the inherited forte and is asked to rise ends one step higher at fortissimo. The trap in the first option is the useful one, since treating a hairpin as a level is a natural mistake. The trap in the second gets the level right and the count wrong, which is what happens when a reader counts the marks at both ends of a hairpin as well as the one the hairpin started from, and that error is worth naming because the two ends of a hairpin are not both written. The trap in the third is the opposite of the truth, since marks persist precisely so that a composer need not write forte under every bar.
questions.hint: A letter mark holds until replaced; a hairpin is a change, not a level. Then count the printed steps.

questions.topic: The interval a trill spans above a written note
questions.learningObjective: name the two auxiliary notes a trill alternates between
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in c major prints a trill sign above a written E4 half note. Which two auxiliary pitches does the trill alternate between, and what does each sign do to the written note?

options.text: The trill alternates between E4 and D4, a major second below the written note, so the lower auxiliary and the principal note are the pair of signs
options.misconception: names the trill as a lower-neighbour alternation

options.text: The trill alternates between F4 and G4, a major third above the written E4, so the two signs are the upper auxiliary and a third above it
options.misconception: reaches for a third above rather than the adjacent auxiliary

options.text: The trill alternates between F4, a minor second above the written E4, and the written E4 itself, so the two signs add the upper auxiliary and restore the principal note without ever leaving a half step
The trill alternates between E4 and E5, a perfect octave above the written note, so the two signs are the written note and the note an octave up
options.misconception: treats a trill as an octave alternation

questions.explanation: The auxiliary of a note is its immediate diatonic neighbour, so for a written E4 the upper auxiliary is F4 and the lower auxiliary is D4, and a trill is the rapid alternation of the written note with the upper auxiliary. Nothing about the ornament goes outside a second, which is what keeps it audible as a decoration of one note rather than as a change of pitch, and the size of that second depends on the letters involved: E to F is a half step because those letters are adjacent on the piano, while C to D is a whole step. The trill sign itself, a tr or a turn-like zigzag, adds the trill to the note it stands over, so the written E4 is replaced by an alternation of E4 and F4 for the whole of its written value, and the duration is unchanged. The choice of the upper auxiliary is not arbitrary, since a trill on a note with a sharp, a flat or a natural is only legible if the auxiliary is spelled and accented correctly, and a composer who needs a lower trill says so with a different sign. The trap in the second option is the most common over-reach, and the octave in the fourth option is a different ornament entirely, an octave sign.
questions.hint: The auxiliary is the neighbouring letter, so the upper auxiliary of E4 is the F above it.

questions.topic: The number of note attacks in a written trill
questions.learningObjective: count the note attacks a trill of a given rate produces
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in c major marks a written C5 whole note with a trill, the ornament is played as equal written and auxiliary notes in alternation, and the trill is played at the rate of four written notes per beat. The whole note is worth four beats, so how many note attacks does the trill produce in all?
questions.explanation: Four written notes per beat over four beats gives 4 times 4, which is 16 attacks, and the arithmetic is a plain multiplication of a rate by a duration. The count has a structure worth naming, because the trill begins on the written note and alternates from there, so with an even number of attacks the last one is the auxiliary and with an odd number it is the written note: 16 attacks means 8 of the written C5 and 8 of the auxiliary D5, and the phrase finishes on the ornament rather than on the principal note. The second half of that observation is why a trill of even length sounds slightly unfinished and why a performer will often make the last pair a single longer written note, which changes the count of attacks without changing the count of alternations. The rate itself is a convention rather than a measurement, and it is set by the tempo, since the same ornament is a shimmer in a slow movement and a blur in a fast one. The trap is 8, which counts the written notes only, and 32, which assumes the auxiliary is itself trilled.
questions.hint: Multiply the rate of four written notes per beat by the four beats of the whole note.

questions.topic: The upper mordent sign
questions.learningObjective: name the pitches a single upper mordent plays
questions.stem: Above a written G4 quarter note in 4/4, common time, in c major, a part prints a short zigzag with a vertical stroke through it. What three pitches does that ornament play, and what is the stroke for?

options.text: It plays G4, then F4, then G4, because the plain zigzag is an upper mordent and the vertical stroke changes the principal note rather than the direction
options.misconception: reads the stroked sign as a lower mordent

options.text: It plays G4, then A4, then G4, because the short zigzag is an upper mordent, and the vertical stroke through it is the sign that distinguishes the upper mordent from the plain zigzag of the lower mordent
It plays G4, then A4, then B4, then C5, because a zigzag ornament always runs upwards through the scale for as many notes as the value allows
options.misconception: treats a mordent as a run of scale notes

options.text: It plays A4, then G4, then A4, because the ornament starts on its auxiliary rather than on the written note
options.misconception: starts the mordent on the auxiliary

questions.explanation: A mordent is a three-note decoration that leaves and returns to the principal note, and the two varieties differ only in which neighbour is used. The plain zigzag is the lower mordent, which dips to the note below and comes back, and the zigzag with a vertical stroke through its middle is the upper mordent, which rises to the note above and comes back. On a written G4 the upper mordent therefore gives G4, A4, G4, three attacks in the time of one written note, and the principal note is both the first and the last, so the ornament resolves onto the note it decorates. The stroke is purely a notational instruction about direction and has no effect on any other parameter, which is worth saying because it is the only difference between the two signs. The trap in the first option reverses the stroke's meaning, and the third inverts the ornament so that it starts away from the written note, which is what a trill does rather than what a mordent does.
questions.hint: The vertical stroke marks the upper mordent, so the ornament rises a step and returns.

questions.topic: The lower mordent sign
questions.learningObjective: name the pitches a plain zigzag mordent plays
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in f major prints a plain short zigzag with no stroke above a written A4 quarter note. What three pitches does that ornament play, and how does its effect differ from the same ornament with a vertical stroke?

options.text: It plays A4, then G4, then A4, because the plain zigzag is the lower mordent, and the stroked version rises to the note above the written note instead of dipping to the note below
It plays A4, then B4, then A4, because the plain zigzag is the upper mordent and only the stroked version dips below the written note
options.misconception: reverses which stroke means which mordent

options.text: It plays A4, then G4, then A4, and the stroked version plays the same three pitches more quickly
options.misconception: believes the stroke changes only the rate

options.text: It plays A4, then Bb4, then A4, because an unstroked zigzag always takes the note above the written note and f major supplies the flat on the letter B
options.misconception: picks the wrong auxiliary pitch

questions.explanation: The two mordents are distinguished by a single stroke, and what that stroke selects is the direction of the single step. Without the stroke the ornament dips, so a written A4 is decorated as A4, G4, A4, and with the stroke it rises, giving A4, B4, A4. The two forms differ in nothing else: each is three attacks in the time of one written note, each begins and ends on the written note, and neither changes the duration of that note. The direction is audible because a dip and a rise colour the principal note differently, and in the Baroque practice that produced both signs the dip was the commoner and the rise the more decorative, which is why the plain zigzag is the more frequent sign in older sources and why the stroked form needs naming rather than recognition. The check against the key fixes the spelling, since the diatonic second below A4 in f major is the G4 that the signature already supplies flat-free, while a G sharp would not belong to the key at all. The trap in the second option is the belief that a stroke is a tempo instruction, when the rate of a mordent is set by the note it decorates rather than by its sign.
questions.hint: No stroke means the ornament dips to the lower neighbour and returns.

questions.topic: The turn over a written note
questions.learningObjective: name the four pitches of a turn in order
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in d major prints a turn sign, the horizontal S-shaped symbol also called a gruppetto, above a written A4 quarter note. What four pitches does the turn play, in what order, and where does the written note sit within them?

options.text: It plays A4, B4, C5, B4, which is the written note, the note above, a third above and the note above again
options.misconception: runs the turn upwards instead of around the note

options.text: It plays B4, C5, D5, C5, which is the note above, a third above, a fifth above and back, since a turn covers four consecutive scale degrees
options.misconception: counts the turn as four steps of a run

options.text: It plays A4, G4, F4, G4, which is the written note, the note below, a third below and back, since a turn descends before it returns
options.misconception: descends from the written note rather than circling it

options.text: It plays B4, A4, G4, A4, which is the upper neighbour, the written note, the lower neighbour and the written note again, so the principal note occupies the second and the fourth of the four attacks

questions.explanation: A turn circles the written note, and the standard form goes up first: the upper auxiliary, the principal note, the lower auxiliary, and the principal note again. On a written A4 that is B4, A4, G4, A4, four attacks in the time of the written note, with the A4 heard twice and once at the end so that the ornament resolves onto its own note. The upper-first ordering is a convention and the other order exists, but the composer who wants it writes a different sign, so the printed S-shaped symbol has one reading. The relation of a turn to a trill is worth keeping separate, because a trill decorates a note by alternating with its upper auxiliary for as long as the note lasts, while a turn decorates it with one fixed four-note figure in one short passage, and a turn is therefore counted rather than sustained. The check against the key is easy, since A4, B4 and G4 are all members of d major, which has two sharps. The trap in the fourth option gives the descending form, and the second gives a four-note run, which is a different ornament entirely.
questions.hint: The turn goes to the upper neighbour, back to the written note, down to the lower neighbour, and back again.

questions.topic: The inverted turn
questions.learningObjective: name the four pitches of an inverted turn in order
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in f major prints an inverted turn sign, the gruppetto turned upside down, above a written C5 quarter note. What four pitches does it play, and which of them is the principal note?

options.text: It plays D5, C5, Bb4, C5, which is the upper neighbour, the written note, the lower neighbour and the written note, so the ordinary turn is the one being asked for
options.misconception: gives the ordinary turn in place of the inverted one

options.text: It plays C5, D5, E5, D5, which is the written note, the note above, a third above and back, since an inverted turn still begins on the written note
options.misconception: starts the inverted turn on the principal note

options.text: It plays Bb4, C5, D5, C5, which is the lower neighbour, the written note, the upper neighbour and the written note again, so C5 occupies the second and the fourth attacks
It plays B4, C5, D5, C5, but the four attacks replace the written note entirely and the written quarter note is therefore omitted
options.misconception: believes the ornament removes the written note and spells the neighbour as a natural

questions.explanation: An inverted turn is the mirror image of the ordinary turn, and the mirror operation is exactly a reversal of the first two steps, so an ordinary turn that goes upper, principal, lower, principal becomes, when inverted, lower, principal, upper, principal. On a written C5 that is Bb4, C5, D5, C5, and the written note still occupies the second and the fourth attacks, which is the invariant that both turn forms share. The Bb4 is spelled with a flat because f major sharpens nothing and flattens the letter B, so the lower neighbour of C5 in that key is the B flat and not the B natural, and the same point applies to the trill's auxiliary on any note whose neighbour the signature has already altered. The sign is drawn by turning the S-shaped gruppetto upside down, and that single change of orientation is the whole of the notational difference, so a reader who can read one turn can read both once the reversal is understood. What the two forms do not differ in is duration or pitch content, since each is four attacks inside the written note's own value and each uses the same two neighbours. The trap in the first option is the ordinary turn, and it is worth noticing that the two options differ only in the order of the first and third attacks, which is exactly the size of the notational difference. The trap in the third is the confusion between the ornament and the note it decorates.
questions.hint: Inverting a turn reverses its opening step, so the lower neighbour comes first.

questions.topic: The appoggiatura and the time it borrows
questions.learningObjective: state where an appoggiatura takes its time from and which note loses it
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in e flat major prints a small grace note, a semiquaver with a slash through its stem, on the beat before a written Bb4 half note. Which written note gives up the time, and what is the sounding result?

options.text: The written Bb4 gives up the time and is then omitted entirely, so the phrase contains only the grace note and no principal note at all
options.misconception: believes the principal note is replaced rather than shortened

options.text: The written Bb4 gives up the time, so the slashed grace note sounds immediately before the beat and the Bb4 begins partway through its own written value, giving one attack on the beat and a shorter principal note after it
The written Bb4 gives up no time, so the slashed grace note is played after the principal note within the same written value
options.misconception: places the slashed grace note after rather than before the beat

options.text: The following written note gives up the time, so the Bb4 sounds at full length and the grace note is taken out of the note that follows it
options.misconception: takes the time from the following note instead

questions.explanation: A slashed grace note is an acciaccatura, and its defining property is where its time comes from: it is played on the beat and it takes its duration from the principal note that follows it, not from the note before. On a written Bb4 half note worth two beats the grace note is heard first, the principal note then begins within that two-beat slot, and the phrase therefore begins with a dissonance that resolves on the beat, which is the expressive point of the ornament. The second option describes the unslashed grace note, the long appoggiatura, which takes its time from the *previous* note instead and therefore falls before the beat, and the two are told apart by the stroke through the stem. The trap in the first option is the commonest misreading, because a notation that looks like an extra note invites the idea that the written note has been replaced, whereas the written note is still there and is simply shortened. The trap in the third reverses the borrowing direction, which is the whole difference between the slashed and unslashed forms.
questions.hint: A slashed grace note takes its time from the principal note it precedes.

questions.topic: The interval an appoggiatura leans against its note
questions.learningObjective: name the interval between an appoggiatura and its resolution
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in c major prints an appoggiatura on the upper auxiliary of a written G4 half note, so the ornament sounds A4 and resolves to the written G4. What interval do the two sounds form, and which of the two is on the beat?

options.text: They form a descending major second, two semitones, from A4 down to G4, and the G4 is on the beat because the appoggiatura is taken before it out of the written note's own time
They form a descending minor second, one semitone, from A4 down to G4, and the G4 is on the beat because the appoggiatura is taken before it
options.misconception: miscounts the second between A4 and G4

options.text: They form a descending major second, two semitones, and the A4 is on the beat because the appoggiatura is the note the ear waits for
options.misconception: puts the appoggiatura on the beat

options.text: They form an ascending major second, two semitones, from G4 up to A4, and the G4 is on the beat because the written note comes first
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the resolution

questions.explanation: The interval an appoggiatura forms with its resolution is a second, and its direction is down, because an appoggiatura leans against the note it resolves to. On a written G4 the upper auxiliary is A4, and A4 down to G4 is two semitones, which is a major second, and the letters A down to G are a second as well, so the number and the size agree. What makes it an appoggiatura rather than an ornament is which of the two lands on the beat: the G4 does, because the appoggiatura has been taken out of the G4's own written time, and the ear therefore registers a dissonance arriving early and a consonance arriving on the beat. The trap in the first option is a genuine counting slip, since the whole step between A and G is easy to mistake for a semitone in isolation, but the second option's placement is right and its size wrong. The trap in the third reverses the direction, which would describe the ornament heard backwards, and the trap in the second puts the dissonance on the beat, which would destroy exactly the effect the ornament exists to create.
questions.hint: A4 down to G4: count the semitones and the letters, and decide which sound lands on the beat.

questions.topic: The grace note written without a stroke
questions.learningObjective: state where an unstroked grace note takes its time from
questions.stem: A small grace note with no stroke through its stem stands on the beat of a written F4 half note in 4/4, common time, in f major, and the note before the grace note is a written A4 half note. Which written note supplies the grace note's time, and where does the grace note fall relative to the beat?

options.text: The written F4 supplies the time, and the grace note falls on the beat, which is the same instruction as a slashed grace note
options.misconception: treats the unstroked grace note as an acciaccatura

options.text: The written A4 supplies the time, and the grace note falls on the beat, since an unstroked grace note is the shorter of the two forms
options.misconception: puts the unstroked grace note on the beat

options.text: Neither note supplies the time, and the grace note is played in whatever silence the tempo allows, since a grace note has no fixed duration
options.misconception: denies that a grace note takes time from anywhere

options.text: The written A4 before it supplies the time, and the grace note falls before the beat, which is the long appoggiatura and the reason it is sometimes written with a value of its own

questions.explanation: The stroke through a grace note's stem is the whole of the distinction between the two grace-note forms, and it changes where the time comes from. A small note with no stroke is the long appoggiatura: it is taken out of the note *preceding* the principal note, so here the written A4 loses the time and the grace note sounds before the beat, arriving early on a dissonance that resolves on the beat at the F4. A small note with a stroke is the acciaccatura, which is taken out of the principal note's own time and so sounds on the beat itself. That is why the long form is often printed with a real note value, since it needs a length and a length needs a note value, whereas the short form is nearly always a semiquaver or a thirty-second. The trap in the first option is the reversal, and it is the commonest because the two forms look almost identical in small type. The trap in the second has the time-borrowing right and the beat wrong, and the third denies the mechanism the ornament is defined by.
questions.hint: No stroke means the previous note gives up the time, so the ornament falls before the beat.

questions.topic: The total time consumed by a turn
questions.learningObjective: compute the sounding time a four-note ornament takes
questions.stem: Four equal attacks that together fill a written note are played in place of a turn, and a turn stands above a written G4 quarter note in 4/4, common time, in c major. How many beats does each of the four attacks last, to three decimal places?
questions.explanation: Four equal attacks inside a written quarter note divide one beat by four, which is 0.25 beats each, and the check is that the four must add back to the whole: 4 times 0.25 is 1.00, the full written value. The division is exact rather than approximate because a turn is a counted figure, which is the practical difference between it and a trill: a trill's rate is a convention that has to be chosen, while a turn's four attacks are forced once the written value is known. The note that the figure sits on keeps its own written value in the score, so a player reading the bar counts the same number of beats whether the note carries a turn, a mordent or nothing at all, and the ornament is absorbed entirely inside the note it decorates. The pitch content is unchanged by any of this, so a turn on a written G4 in c major still uses only B4, G4 and F4 and needs no accidental. The trap is 0.5, which is the value a two-note ornament such as a single appoggiatura would occupy, and 0.125, which would be the result of dividing by eight.
questions.hint: Divide the written quarter note, one beat, by the four attacks of the turn.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that realises a turn
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that returns the four pitches of a turn in order
questions.stem: Trace the rule turn(w), which returns the four pitches of a turn above a written note, from the upper neighbour down: turn(w) = return [up(w), w, down(w), w], where up(w) is the note a diatonic second above w and down(w) is the note a diatonic second below w. Apply it to a written E4 quarter note in 4/4, common time, in c major. What four pitches does the rule return?

options.text: D4, E4, F4, E4, since the rule returns the lower neighbour first because a turn descends before it ascends
options.misconception: inverts the order the rule states

options.text: F4, G4, E4, D4, since up(w) means a diatonic second and the rule climbs through the scale from the upper neighbour
options.misconception: reads a second as a step upwards through the scale

options.text: F4, E4, D4, E4, since the diatonic second above E4 is F4 and the diatonic second below E4 is D4, so the figure is the upper neighbour, the written note, the lower neighbour and the written note
E4, F4, E4, D4, since the written note comes first so that the ornament ends on its lower neighbour
options.misconception: puts the principal note at the start of the figure

questions.explanation: The rule is a list with four entries and the only work is filling the two helpers, which is a question of letters rather than of semitones. The diatonic second above E4 is F4, since a second means the next letter, and the diatonic second below E4 is D4, and the two are not the same size, because E to F happens to be a half step while E down to D is a whole tone, which is exactly why a trill's auxiliary is chosen by letter and not by semitone count. The list then reads F4, E4, D4, E4, with the written note in the second and the fourth positions, which is the invariant that makes the figure sound like a turn rather than like a run. The key check passes without an accidental, since c major has none and E4, F4 and D4 are all its members. The trap in the first option is the most likely misreading of a rule that is written explicitly, and it is worth noticing that the two lists contain exactly the same three pitches and differ only in order, which is precisely the difference between a turn and an inverted turn. The trap in the second confuses a diatonic second with a scale step upwards, and the third ignores the literal order of the list.
questions.hint: A diatonic second is the next letter name up or down, so work out F4 and D4 and then read the list.

questions.topic: The figure written over a pair of notes
questions.learningObjective: name the figure a turn placed between two notes plays
questions.stem: In 4/4, common time, in c major, a turn sign is printed in the gap between a written C5 quarter note and a written D5 quarter note, so that the figure joins the two notes rather than sitting on either of them. What five pitches does the passage sound, and why is the third of them not the upper neighbour of the C5?

options.text: It sounds C5, D5, C5, D5, C5, because a turn between two notes alternates the two notes themselves and adds no third pitch
options.misconception: reads the between-notes turn as an alternation of the two notes

options.text: It sounds C5, D5, E5, D5, C5, because a turn written between two notes decorates the interval between them and works backwards from the second note, so the E5 is the upper neighbour of the D5 that follows rather than of the C5 that precedes
It sounds D5, C5, B4, C5, D5, because the figure is an inverted turn of the gap and so descends before it ascends
options.misconception: inverts a between-notes turn

options.text: It sounds C5, D5, E5, F5, E5, because the figure climbs a scale from the first note towards the second
options.misconception: treats the figure as a scale run

questions.explanation: A turn changes its reference note depending on where it is printed, and that is the whole of the difference between the two uses. A turn printed *over* a note decorates that note and circles it. A turn printed *between* two notes decorates the interval between them, and it works backwards from the note that follows: the principal note is the second of the pair, the figure is that note's upper neighbour, the second note itself, its lower neighbour, and then the second note again, after which the first note of the pair is heard. On a written C5 followed by a written D5 that gives C5, D5, E5, D5, C5. The E5 is a diatonic second above the D5, not above the C5, which is exactly the point the question turns on, and the letter difference is what shows it: a second above C5 is D5, so E5 cannot be the upper neighbour of the C5. The trap in the first option reduces the ornament to an alternation, and the second applies the inverted turn's order, and the third turns the whole figure into a scale.
questions.hint: A turn between two notes works from the second note: its upper neighbour, itself, its lower neighbour, itself.

questions.topic: The trill auxiliary when the key signature has already sharpened the neighbour
questions.learningObjective: name a trill auxiliary that the key signature does not supply
questions.stem: A trill sign stands above a written F sharp 4 half note in 4/4, common time, in e major, whose signature has four sharps and supplies the sharp on the letter F. The auxiliary of a note is its diatonic second above, so the letter above F is G. Which pitch does the trill use as its auxiliary, and what does the composer have to print to make it unambiguous?

options.text: The auxiliary is G4, a minor second above the written F sharp 4, and because e major's signature sharpens the letter G as well as F, a natural has to be printed in front of the G so that the player does not read the signature's G sharp
The auxiliary is G sharp 4, a major second above the written F sharp 4, because the key signature already sharpens the letter G and needs no cancelling sign
options.misconception: follows the signature blindly and takes the wrong letter

options.text: The auxiliary is E4, a whole tone below the written F sharp 4, because the letter below F is E and an unbarred trill sign takes the neighbour below
options.misconception: sends the trill to the lower neighbour

options.text: The auxiliary is G4 and nothing has to be printed in front of it, because a key signature can never conflict with the auxiliary of an ornament
options.misconception: believes a signature can never collide with an ornament

questions.explanation: The auxiliary of a note is its diatonic second above, which fixes the letter and not the accidental, and for a written F sharp 4 the letter above is G. The size of the second then depends on the accidentals in play: F sharp 4 up to G natural is one semitone, a minor second, while F sharp 4 up to G sharp is two semitones, a major second. Both are diatonic seconds above the letter F, and the notation has to say which, because e major's signature puts a sharp on the letter G as well as on F and a C. A composer who wants the trill to sound with the natural G must therefore print a natural in front of the auxiliary, and that is a real and frequent editorial decision rather than a detail, since the alternative is a trill a whole tone wider than intended. The trap in the first option is the one this item is built around, because a player who reads the signature mechanically will hear G sharp and a composer who does not check will get the same result. The trap in the second option confuses a trill with a lower mordent, which is a different ornament with a different sign, and the third denies that the two systems can collide at all, which is the situation the item is built on.
questions.hint: Fix the letter first, then ask what the key signature does to that letter before deciding the accidental.

questions.topic: The figured bass symbol for a root position triad
questions.learningObjective: identify the figure that stands for a root position triad
questions.stem: A continuo part in 4/4, common time, in c major is given a bass line and a figure, and the player must supply the harmony above it. What does the bare figure, no numbers at all, tell the player to build above the written bass note?

options.text: It tells the player to build a triad with the written bass note as its fifth, since a blank figure leaves the inversion to the player and the bass note is the chord fifth
options.misconception: reads a blank figure as a second inversion

options.text: It tells the player to build only a single note a third above the bass, since a blank figure supplies no interval at all
options.misconception: treats a blank figure as supplying nothing

options.text: It tells the player to build a triad with the written bass note as its third, since figured bass numbers the intervals above the bass and a blank leaves the first interval unstated
options.misconception: reads a blank figure as a first inversion

options.text: It tells the player to build a triad with the written bass note as its root, stacking a third and a fifth above it, and a blank figure means root position because unfigured bass implies the most ordinary chord

questions.explanation: Figured bass works by giving the intervals above the bass that are not the octave, and the case that needs no figures at all is the one where every interval follows from convention. A root position triad has a third and a fifth above the bass, and a fifth is the default, so the only interval that actually needs stating is the third, and a figure of six three states it while a blank figure states nothing because the third is assumed. That is why a blank means root position: the harmony is the plainest available, and continuo players read a blank as the most idiomatic chord at that bass note. The general rule behind the notation is worth stating because it explains every other figure: a figure names the intervals above the bass in the order they appear, and the intervals are counted from the bass rather than from the root, which is why six three is a first inversion and not a second. The trap in the first option is the standard confusion between the bass note and the root, and they coincide only in root position. The trap in the third is a plausible but wrong reading of what a figure counts.
questions.hint: A blank figure means the third and fifth above the bass are both assumed, which is a root position triad.
