questions.topic: The figured bass symbol for a first inversion
questions.learningObjective: identify the figure that stands for a first inversion triad
questions.stem: A continuo part in 4/4, common time, in c major prints a bass note of E3 with the figure six three beneath it. What chord do the bass note and the figure produce, and which member of the chord is in the bass?

options.text: It produces the triad on E, that is E4, G4 and C5, with the E3 in the bass, so the root of the chord is lowest and the chord is in root position
options.misconception: takes the bass note as the root and ignores the figure

options.text: It produces the triad on G, that is G3, C4 and E4, with the E3 above the root, so the chord is in second inversion
options.misconception: reads six three as a second inversion

options.text: It produces the triad on C, that is C4, E4 and G4, with the E3 in the bass, so the third of the chord is lowest and the chord is in first inversion
It produces the triad on C with a doubled bass, so the E3 sounds twice at the same octave and the figure adds nothing
options.misconception: believes a figure adds a doubling

questions.explanation: A figure states the intervals above the bass, counted from the bass, and six three says that a sixth and a third lie above the written note. A sixth above E3 is C4, since E3 up to C4 is six letter names and eight semitones, and a third above E3 is G3, so the three pitches are E3, G3 and C4, which is a C major triad with its third in the bass. The chord member in the bass is therefore the third, and that is the definition of first inversion. The number six rather than three is the giveaway, because a third above a bass note that is a chord's third lies a sixth above the actual root, and a figure always measures from what is written rather than from the root. The trap in the first option is the plainest mistake in the whole subject, treating the bass note as the root, and the second misreads the inversion figure in the opposite direction, since a six four is what indicates a second inversion.
questions.hint: A sixth and a third above E3: work out the two pitches and then name the chord they belong to.

questions.topic: The figured bass symbol for a second inversion
questions.learningObjective: identify the figure that stands for a second inversion triad
questions.stem: Beneath a bass note of G3 in 4/4, common time, in c major, a continuo part prints the figure six four. What chord do the bass note and the figure produce, and which member of the chord is in the bass?

options.text: It produces the triad on G, that is G4, B4 and D5, with the G3 in the bass, so the root of the chord is lowest and the figure is redundant
options.misconception: takes the bass note as the root and ignores the figure

options.text: It produces the triad on C, that is C4, E4 and G4, with the G3 in the bass, so the fifth of the chord is lowest and the chord is in second inversion
It produces the triad on C with the E4 in the bass, since a four above the bass names the root and the chord is therefore in first inversion
options.misconception: reads six four as a first inversion

options.text: It produces the triad on C in root position, since six four and six three name the same three pitches from different starting points
options.misconception: believes the two figures are interchangeable

questions.explanation: Six four over a written G3 asks for a fourth and a sixth above the bass, and a fourth above G3 is C4 while a sixth above G3 is E4, so the sounding pitches are G3, C4 and E4, which is a C major triad with its fifth in the bass. That is the definition of second inversion, and the pair of figures is worth tabulating because the pattern is regular: five three or a blank for root position, six three for a third in the bass, and six four for a fifth in the bass. The numbers are always counted up from the written bass, which is why a first inversion shows a six and a second inversion shows a four. The reason a second inversion is written six four rather than just four is that a fourth alone would leave the third ambiguous, since a fourth above the bass is a third above the root and a sixth above the bass is a third above the bass, and giving both removes the doubt. The trap in the first option is the bass-equals-root error again, and the third is the useful one, because the two figures do name the same three pitches of the same chord and differ only in which one is written lowest.
questions.hint: A fourth and a sixth above G3 give C4 and E4, which with G3 make a C major triad over its fifth.

questions.topic: A sharp written beneath a figured bass symbol
questions.learningObjective: say what a sharp beneath a figure alters and which column it belongs to
questions.stem: Beneath a bass note of E3 in 4/4, common time, in c major, a continuo part prints the figure six sharp three, that is a six, then a sharp, then a three. Which three pitches does the player sound, and which column does the sharp belong to?

options.text: The player sounds E3, G sharp 3 and C4, which is an augmented C major triad in first inversion, and the sharp belongs to the three, because it stands directly above that number and so raises the third above the bass from the G natural that the key of c major would otherwise supply
The player sounds E3, G4 and C4, which is a C major triad in first inversion, because the sharp stands above the three and so raises the third above the bass to the G sharp that c major lacks
options.misconception: raises the right note but calls the result a C major triad

options.text: The player sounds E3, C4 and G sharp 4, because the sharp stands above the six and so raises the note a sixth above the bass rather than the third
options.misconception: attaches the sharp to the six rather than the three

options.text: The player sounds E sharp 3, G sharp 3 and C4, because a sharp written in a figure alters the bass note as well as the interval above it
options.misconception: applies the sharp to the bass as well

questions.explanation: An accidental printed in a figure belongs to the column it stands over, and the columns are read upwards from the bass, so in six sharp three the sharp sits over the three and not over the six. A third above the written E3 is G3, which in c major would be the G natural the key already provides, and the sharp raises that to G sharp 3. A sixth above the written E3 is C4, and no accidental is written over the six, so the C4 stands as the key gives it. The three sounding pitches are therefore E3, G sharp 3 and C4, and those are the three tones of a C augmented triad with its third in the bass, since the C major triad is C, E, G and the raised G turns the fifth into a G sharp. The second option's reading, in which the sharp belongs to the six, is the trap this notation is designed to catch, and it happens whenever a continuo player reads the figure as a chord label rather than as a set of columns. A shortened figure is also worth knowing, since a sharp standing alone always means a raised third, a six alone means six three, and a figure that reduces to nothing means a root position triad.
questions.hint: Read the figure as columns upwards from the bass: the six sits over the bass and the sharp over the three below it.

questions.topic: Roman numerals as analysis rather than as figured bass
questions.learningObjective: tell an analysis label apart from a continuo figure
questions.stem: A scholar prints a numeral six four under a written G3 in 4/4, common time, in c major, and separately a continuo player prints six four under the same written G3. What does each reader do with the numeral, and why can the two not be interchanged?

options.text: Both readers do the same thing, because six four under a bass note always means a second inversion triad and the two systems are simply synonyms
options.misconception: believes analysis and continuo figures are interchangeable

options.text: The scholar uses six four to mean a third and a sixth above the bass while the continuo player uses it to name the inversion, so the roles are the opposite of what they appear
options.misconception: swaps the roles of the two systems

options.text: Neither reader needs the numeral, because a bass note of G3 with no other information already fixes the chord in c major
options.misconception: believes the bass note alone determines the chord

options.text: The scholar uses six four as an analysis label naming a second inversion chord on the first degree, so the number describes the chord and its bass, while the continuo player uses it as intervals to be played above the bass, so the numbers describe what to sound

questions.explanation: The two systems use the same numerals for different jobs, and the difference is what the numbers are measured from. Figured bass measures upward from the written bass, so six four asks for intervals to be sounded above it. A Roman-numeral analysis measures from the key, so the figure is attached to a numeral naming a scale degree and its inversion, and the numbers that follow it describe the spacing above the bass. The collision is real and it is why figured bass is usually written under the bass line while an analysis is written above or below a reduction, and why a continuo player and a harmonic analyst can look at the same page and read different things. The trap in the first option is the natural one, since the notation genuinely looks identical and the two systems did grow out of the same practice. The trap in the second is the exact reversal, and the third overstates what a bass note can determine, since a single bass note belongs to several chords at once and the figure is what removes that ambiguity.
questions.hint: One system measures upwards from the bass and one measures from the key, and that difference decides what the numbers mean.

questions.topic: Fingering numbers on a keyboard part
questions.learningObjective: say what a keyboard fingering number instructs
questions.stem: A piano part in 4/4, common time, in c major prints a small 4 above a written F4 quarter note and a small 1 above a written C5 quarter note. What do those two numbers instruct, and what do they leave the player to decide?

options.text: They instruct the player to play those notes on the fourth and first beats of the bar, and they leave the choice of pitch to the notes themselves
options.misconception: reads a fingering number as a metrical position

options.text: They instruct the player to play those two notes as a pair, since two numbers over two notes always mark a chord
options.misconception: reads two fingering numbers as a chord instruction

options.text: They instruct the player to use the fourth finger and the thumb on those two notes, and they leave the choice of which other fingers play the notes in between entirely to the player
They instruct the player to use the fourth and first fingers on every occurrence of those pitches in the piece, and they leave no discretion at all
options.misconception: treats a fingering number as applying throughout the piece

questions.explanation: A fingering number counts fingers rather than beats, and the numbering is fixed by convention: the thumb is one and the little finger is five, with the remaining three numbered across the hand. The two marks therefore say play this F4 with finger four and this C5 with finger one, which is the advice a composer or editor gives to keep a passage in the most comfortable hand position, and the reason a mark is often placed on the first and last notes of a run rather than on every note, since the hand position is what matters and the rest follows. The marks are local to the passage, which is what the third option gets wrong, and they are a suggestion in the sense that an advanced player will depart from them when the musical result is better for it. The trap in the first option is the ordinary ambiguity of a bare numeral, and the second is the assumption that numbers stacked over notes always mean a chord, which is a reasonable guess in a different notation.
questions.hint: The numbers count fingers, and the thumb is one and the little finger is five.

questions.topic: Reading a table of continuo figures against their chords
questions.learningObjective: match continuo figures to the chords and inversions they produce
questions.stem: A table of continuo figures in 4/4, common time, in c major gives four rows. Row one: bass E3, figure six three. Row two: bass G3, figure six four. Row three: bass C3, no figure. Row four: bass G3, no figure. Which two rows put the root of their chord in the bass, and which three rows produce the same three pitch classes?

options.text: Row one puts the root in the bass, since the six names the third of the chord and a third in the bass is the root of a first inversion triad
options.misconception: identifies a first inversion as a root position

options.text: Rows three and four put the root in the bass, since a blank figure with a bass of C3 gives the C major triad and a blank figure with a bass of G3 gives the G major triad, and rows one, two and three all produce the pitch classes C, E and G
Rows three and four put the root in the bass, and no two rows produce the same three pitch classes, since each figure gives a different set of intervals above its own bass
options.misconception: believes two rows cannot name one chord

options.text: Rows one and two put the root in the bass, since a figure of six three and a figure of six four both name the triad that the bass note belongs to
options.misconception: takes every bass note as the root

questions.explanation: The table is read one row at a time, and each row's job is to name the intervals above its own bass. Row three is the easy case: a blank figure over a bass of C3 gives C3, E3 and G3, a C major triad with its root lowest, and the same reasoning gives G3, B3 and D4 for row four, a G major triad with its root lowest. Row one gives a third and a sixth above E3, which are G3 and C4, and row two gives a fourth and a sixth above G3, which are C4 and E4, so rows one and two are both the C major triad with the bass note taken from a different chord member. Sorting the four rows by bass role therefore separates the two root positions from the two inversions, and sorting them by pitch content shows that rows one, two and three all name C, E and G while row four alone names G, B and D. That is the point the table is built to make, because a continuo part is full of figures over bass notes that belong to several chords at once, and the figure is what says which. The trap in the first option misnames a first inversion, and the third makes the bass-equals-root error on the two rows where the bass is a chord member but not the root.
questions.hint: Build each row from its own bass and figure, then sort the rows by which chord member the bass note turns out to be.

questions.topic: The number of times a section with a repeat sign is played
questions.learningObjective: count the performances of a section bounded by repeat signs
questions.stem: A movement in 4/4, common time, in g major opens with a bar line carrying a forward repeat sign, closes that section with a backward repeat sign, and then continues into material that is not repeated. The repeated section is eight bars long. How many bars of that section are performed in total?
questions.explanation: A repeated section is performed twice, so an eight-bar section under repeat signs sounds sixteen bars, and the arithmetic is eight plus eight. The two repeat signs are doing different jobs and both are needed, because the forward repeat at the start marks where the passage begins and the backward repeat at its end marks where it returns to, and it is the backward sign alone that produces the second performance. That is why a passage can carry a forward repeat without a backward one, in which case it is simply a marker of a structural division and nothing is played twice. The check against the metre confirms that nothing about the bar count changes: each of the eight bars still contains four beats on both passes, and the repeat is a matter of performing the same written bars again rather than of altering their content. A third performance would need a pair of repeat signs with dots, and the trap of 8 is the reading in which the section plays once, and the trap of 24 is the reading in which a dotted repeat is assumed.
questions.hint: A repeated section plays twice, so double the eight bars.

questions.topic: A da capo and the length of a performance
questions.learningObjective: compute the length of a performance with a da capo
questions.stem: A rondo in 4/4, common time, in g major has an opening section of sixteen bars, a middle section of twenty-four bars, and a closing section of sixteen bars, and the closing section is marked da capo, which returns to the start. How many bars are performed in all?
questions.explanation: The two outer sections each run sixteen bars and the middle runs twenty-four, so the first pass is 16 plus 24 plus 16, which is 56. The da capo then returns to the start and replays the opening, 16 bars, and the movement stops there, giving 56 plus 16, which is 72. The arithmetic is worth writing out in that order because the mistake people make is adding three sections twice, which would give 112 and would require the da capo to send the players back to the very beginning of the movement rather than to the point the closing section had already reached. What a da capo returns to is the start of the piece, and since the closing section is the third section the return replays only the first section before the movement ends. The check against the metre is that every bar in every section is still four beats, and a da capo changes the order of performance without changing a single written bar. The trap of 56 is the performance without the da capo, and the trap of 112 treats the instruction as a repeat of the whole movement.
questions.hint: Add the three sections once, then add the opening section again for the da capo.

questions.topic: The segno sign and where it returns to
questions.learningObjective: locate the bar a segno returns the performance to
questions.stem: A movement in 4/4, common time, in c major places a segno sign at the start of bar nine, a dal segno at the start of bar twenty-five, and a coda after bar thirty-two. Which bar does the player return to, and how many bars separate the two marks?

options.text: The player returns to bar nine, the bar carrying the segno, and the two marks are sixteen bars apart, since twenty-five minus nine is sixteen
The player returns to bar one, and the two marks are twenty-four bars apart, since a segno is a sign that sends the player back to the beginning of the movement
options.misconception: treats a segno as a da capo

options.text: The player returns to bar twenty-five, and the two marks are sixteen bars apart, since the sign is printed on the bar that receives the repeat
options.misconception: returns to the sign marking the jump rather than the sign marking the target

options.text: The player returns to bar nine and the two marks are sixteen bars apart, but the coda after bar thirty-two is then never reached because the return comes after it
options.misconception: puts the coda after the repeat instruction

questions.explanation: A segno is a sign that marks a point worth returning to, and a dal segno is the instruction that sends the player back to it, so the two marks form a matched pair and the target is always the segno and never the dal segno itself. The distance between them is the part of the movement that is played twice, and here it is twenty-five minus nine, which is sixteen bars. The coda then adds material that is played only once at the end, after the return, so the order of performance is bars one to eight, nine to twenty-four, twenty-five to thirty-two, the coda's bars, then nine to twenty-four again, twenty-five to thirty-two again and the coda again. That is the mechanism a segno provides, and it is what allows a long movement to be written in one pass with a return rather than in two. The trap in the first option confuses the pair with a da capo, which returns to the first bar, and the third is the one worth being careful about, since a coda placed after the repeat instruction would indeed never be reached.
questions.hint: The segno marks the target bar and the dal segno marks the jump, and the gap between them is the repeated span.

questions.topic: Two endings and which one is taken
questions.learningObjective: say how first and second endings are selected in a performance
questions.stem: A minuet in 4/4, common time, in d major is written with a repeat from bar one to bar eight, a first ending over bars nine and ten, and a second ending over bars eleven and twelve. Which ending is played on the first pass, and what happens on the second?

options.text: The second ending is played on the first pass, then the repeat sends the players back to bar one, and on the second pass the first ending is taken
options.misconception: reverses which ending comes first

options.text: Both endings are played on every pass, since each is a written section that must be performed and a repeat sign replays every written bar
options.misconception: believes a repeat replays the endings as well as the section

options.text: The first ending is played on both passes and the second ending is never used, since a repeat sign always returns to the bar after the ending it followed
options.misconception: believes the repeat skips the endings

options.text: The first ending is played on the first pass, then the repeat sends the players back to bar one, and on the second pass the second ending is taken and the repeat sign is not obeyed again

questions.explanation: First and second endings exist so that a repeated section can have two different continuations, and the mechanics are simple once the signs are read as a pair. On the first pass the players meet the first ending, which sends them back to the beginning, and on the second pass they meet the second ending, which does not, so the repeat is not obeyed again and the piece continues. The important consequence is that the repeated span is the first eight bars only, because the endings sit outside the repeat's forward sign in the usual layout, and that is what lets the two endings differ without either one being played twice. The trap in the second option is the natural assumption that a repeat replays everything written, whereas the endings are precisely the mechanism for preventing that, and the trap in the first is a simple reversal. The practical reason composers use the device is tonal: a first ending can lead onwards while a second can arrive on a cadence the repeat made impossible the first time.
questions.hint: The first ending sends the players back and the second one stops them, so the repeat is obeyed once only.

questions.topic: The bar count a multi-bar rest represents
questions.learningObjective: compute the number of bars a multi-bar rest stands for
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in g major shows a whole rest with the number 6 printed above it, and a number 3 above a second rest elsewhere in the same part. How many bars of silence does each of the two signs stand for?
questions.explanation: The number printed above a multi-bar rest is the count of bars, so the 6 stands for six bars and the 3 for three bars, and the figure is read as a count rather than as a note value. The distinction from an ordinary whole rest matters because an ordinary whole rest fills one bar whatever the metre, and in 4/4 that is four beats, while a multi-bar rest with a number is a shorthand for a run of bars that would otherwise need that many rest symbols. The total silence the two signs represent is six plus three, which is nine bars, and at four beats to the bar that is thirty-six beats of written time. The check against the metre confirms the two levels of counting: the 6 and the 3 count bars, and the four beats in each bar come from the metre, so a number of rests and a number of beats are not interchangeable. The trap of 1 is what a reader gives who treats the printed figure as a note value, and the trap of 24 confuses the beat count of the six bars with the bar count itself.
questions.hint: The number above a multi-bar rest counts bars, and each of those bars holds four beats.

questions.topic: A courtesy accidental in a new bar
questions.learningObjective: say what a cautionary accidental does across a bar line
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in c major has a written B flat 4 quarter note in bar one, which the bar's key signature and an accidental supply, and then a written B natural 4 quarter note in bar two, printed with a natural even though c major's signature puts no accidental on the letter B. What does that natural instruct?

options.text: It instructs the player to play the B flat again, because a natural in front of a note cancels the key signature and the key signature of c major contains a B flat
options.misconception: believes c major sharpens or flattens the letter B

options.text: It instructs the player to play the B natural for the rest of the movement, because an accidental once written applies to every later occurrence of the same letter
options.misconception: believes an accidental persists beyond its bar

options.text: It instructs the player to play the B natural, because an accidental lasts only to the end of its bar, so the B flat of bar one has no force in bar two and the natural is written to remove any doubt
It instructs nothing, since c major needs no accidental on the letter B and the sign is therefore redundant
options.misconception: treats the cautionary natural as a mistake

questions.explanation: An accidental has a strictly limited life: it applies to that letter at that octave for the rest of the bar in which it is printed, and it expires at the bar line. The rule exists because a signature already fixes the normal state of each letter, and an accidental is a temporary departure from it, so there is nothing for it to override once the bar has turned. That is what makes the natural in bar two necessary here: the B flat in bar one is a temporary departure from c major's B natural, it expires at the bar line, and the B natural in bar two is simply the letter behaving normally. Such a sign is usually called a cautionary or courtesy accidental, and it is written when a composer wants to remove any chance that a reader will carry the previous bar's accidental forward. The trap in the second option is the opposite error, the belief that an accidental lasts for the whole piece, and the trap in the third mistakes a helpful reminder for an error.
questions.hint: An accidental lasts to the end of its own bar, so the B flat of bar one has no force in bar two.

questions.topic: The accidental needed beyond a key signature of seven sharps
questions.learningObjective: name the accidental required when a note leaves a seven sharp signature
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in c sharp major, whose signature carries seven sharps and already includes a C sharp, needs a note a whole tone above the written B sharp 4. What is that note's scientific pitch name, and what accidental has to stand in front of the letter?

options.text: The note is C double sharp 5, and the accidental has to be a single sharp, because the signature's C sharp plus one further sharp is all that a whole tone above the written B sharp requires
options.misconception: counts one sharp short and so lands a semitone below the intended pitch

options.text: The note is C double sharp 5, and the accidental has to be a double sharp, because the letter above B is C and the required sound is D natural, which lies two semitones above the C natural that the signature already sharpens once
The note is D sharp 5, and the accidental has to be a single sharp, because a note a step above B keeps the letter B and the signature already sharpens that letter
options.misconception: keeps the original letter instead of taking the next one

options.text: The note is D5, and no accidental is needed, because a whole tone above the seventh degree of any major key is that key's tonic
options.misconception: believes a whole tone above the leading note is the tonic

questions.explanation: The scientific pitch name of a note is fixed by its letter and its accidental, and the two jobs have to be done in that order. The letter comes from the notation's need, and for a note a step above a B that letter is C. The pitch comes from the sound, and the required sound is a whole tone above the written B sharp 4, which is D natural, a note that c sharp major does not contain at all. Only then can the accidental be worked out, and the arithmetic is the point of the item: the C natural lies two semitones below the required D natural, so the letter C needs two sharps, and a single sharp on that letter would give the C sharp 5 of the signature, a semitone too low. The consequence is a printed double sharp on a letter the signature has already touched, which is the situation that makes keys with seven sharps hard to read and is one reason they are rare in practice. The trap in the first option is the counting slip, and the second confuses the letter question with the pitch question by keeping the B. The trap in the third is a real and tempting generalisation, and it fails for a specific reason: a semitone above the leading note is the tonic, so a whole tone above it is the supertonic raised, which in c sharp major is the D natural rather than the D sharp.
questions.hint: Fix the letter as C, then ask how far the required sound lies above the C natural, and remember the signature already sharpens that letter once.

questions.topic: Why a raised seventh degree is not spelled as its enharmonic equivalent
questions.learningObjective: say why two enharmonic names for one pitch are not interchangeable
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in a minor, whose key signature carries no accidentals, prints a written G sharp 4 as the raised seventh degree of the scale, a leading note a semitone below the tonic A4. What is that same sounding pitch called, and why must the score not spell it that way instead?

options.text: It is the same sounding pitch as A flat 4, and the score must not use that name because the seventh degree above the tonic keeps the letter G, so a raised seventh is spelled G sharp while an A flat repeats the tonic's own letter and so no longer names the seventh degree at all
It is the same sounding pitch as A flat 4, and the score may use either name, because two names for one sound are simply two labels for the same thing
options.misconception: believes enharmonic names are interchangeable labels

options.text: It is the same sounding pitch as A flat 4, and the score should prefer the flat because a flat is the smaller sign and so is easier to read in a key with no accidentals
options.misconception: chooses the spelling by the shape of the sign

options.text: It is the same sounding pitch as G flat 4, and the score may use either name, because a G flat and a G sharp are one note name with two different accidentals
options.misconception: thinks a change of accidental leaves the pitch alone

questions.explanation: Two note names that sound alike are enharmonic, and the reason they exist at all is that neither letter can serve every function, so the same sound sometimes has to be written two ways. What makes them non-interchangeable is that the letter decides the scale degree, and the scale degree decides the behaviour. A minor's seventh degree has the letter G, because the seventh degree above the tonic A is a G, and that degree appears in two forms: the G natural of the natural minor scale, a whole tone below the tonic, and the G sharp of the harmonic and melodic forms, a semitone below it and therefore a leading note that pulls upwards. The G sharp and the A flat do sound alike, and a score could print the A flat without changing a single pitch; the trouble is that a reader would then see a note carrying the tonic's own letter rather than the seventh's, so the note would no longer announce itself as the leading note and a passage built on that pull would have to be explained in words instead of read. The distance from the tonic cannot separate the two names, since both the G sharp and the A flat are a semitone below the A4, and it is the letter alone that does the work. The trap in the first option treats enharmonic names as synonyms, the second chooses a spelling by the shape of the sign rather than by the function, and the third confuses a change of accidental with a change of nothing at all.
questions.hint: The letter fixes the scale degree, and the scale degree fixes how the note resolves, so the two names are not interchangeable.

questions.topic: The spelling of an augmented fourth
questions.learningObjective: say why a tritone takes different names in different keys
questions.stem: The written F4 and the written B4 are six semitones apart in 4/4, common time, in c major, so the interval is a tritone. What is that interval called, and why is the same tritone a different name when it is spelled F4 to C flat 5?

options.text: Between F4 and B4 it is a diminished fifth, and between F4 and C flat 5 it is an augmented fourth, because a tritone is a fifth when it is narrow and a fourth when it is wide
options.misconception: reverses the two names

options.text: Both are called a tritone, and the letter makes no difference because a tritone is the only name for six semitones
options.misconception: believes tritone is the only permissible name

options.text: Between F4 and B4 it is an augmented fourth, and between F4 and C flat 5 it is also an augmented fourth, because a second spelling of the same interval must keep the same number
options.misconception: believes enharmonic spellings must share a number

options.text: Between F4 and B4 it is an augmented fourth, and between F4 and C flat 5 it is a diminished fifth, because the two spellings put four and five letter names between the endpoints and the letter count fixes the interval number

questions.explanation: An interval's number comes from its letters and its quality from its semitone count, and a tritone is the single size, six semitones, that two different letter spans can produce. F to B is four letter names, so it is a fourth, and four semitones would be a perfect fourth while six semitones widens it, so it is an augmented fourth. F to C is five letter names, so it is a fifth, and a perfect fifth is seven semitones while six narrows it, so it is a diminished fifth. Both are the same sound and they are called different things because the name says how the note behaves: an augmented fourth tends to resolve outwards as a tritone that is part of a dominant seventh, and a diminished fifth tends to resolve inwards as the tritone of a diminished seventh. The trap in the first option is the reversal, the third asserts that enharmonic pairs must agree on the number when they are the definition of a name that does not, and the second is the tritone-equals-a-name confusion that this pair exists to break.
questions.hint: Count the letter names for the number and the semitones for the quality, and the two spellings give different numbers.

questions.topic: The tritone of a dominant seventh beside the tritone of a diminished seventh
questions.learningObjective: say which chord each spelling of a tritone belongs to
questions.stem: In 4/4, common time, in c major, two tritones are at issue. A dominant seventh chord on G has the tones G3, B3, D4 and F4, voiced with the B3 below the F4, and a diminished seventh chord on G has the tones G3, Bb3, Db4 and Fb4, voiced with the Bb3 below the Fb4. Which of the following statements about the two tritones is true? Select every statement that holds.

options.text: The pair B3 and F4 is the tritone of a dominant seventh chord, because in that chord the B is the third and the F is the diminished seventh, and the two lean in opposite directions, the third rising a semitone to the C and the seventh falling a semitone to the E

The pair Bb3 and Fb4 is the tritone of a diminished seventh chord, because in that chord the Bb is the third and the Fb is the diminished seventh, and the two both fall a semitone, the Bb to the A and the Fb to the E flat
The pair B3 and F4 is the tritone of a diminished seventh chord, because a diminished seventh chord is the only chord that contains a tritone
options.misconception: gives the tritone to the wrong chord type

options.text: The pair Bb3 and Fb4 is the tritone of a dominant seventh chord, because a dominant seventh chord always resolves both tritone members downwards
options.misconception: gives the dominant seventh the inward resolution

options.text: Neither pair is a tritone, because a tritone must be spelled as a diminished fifth and a pair spelled as an augmented fourth is a different interval
options.misconception: denies that an augmented fourth is a tritone

questions.explanation: Two of the five statements hold, and the difference between them is the direction the two notes resolve. The tritone of a chord lies between its third and its seventh, so in a dominant seventh chord on G it is the B with the F, and in a diminished seventh chord on G it is the Bb with the Fb; both pairs are six semitones apart, and in the voicing given each is spelled as a diminished fifth. The behaviour then separates them. The dominant seventh's B is the third, and it rises a semitone to the C, while its F is the diminished seventh and it falls a semitone to the E, so the pair leans in opposite directions and that opposition is what gives the dominant seventh its drive. The diminished seventh's Bb is the third and it falls a semitone to the A, and its Fb is the diminished seventh and it falls a semitone to the E flat, so the pair leans the same way, which is why that chord sounds so much more settled. The spelling of the same six semitones also changes with the voicing: put the F4 below the B and the interval becomes F4 up to B4, four letter names and six semitones, which is an augmented fourth rather than a diminished fifth, and the chord is unchanged. The trap in the third option gives the tritone to the wrong chord type, the fourth gives the dominant seventh the inward resolution, and the fifth denies that an augmented fourth is a tritone at all.
questions.hint: Find the tritone between each chord third and its seventh, then ask which way each of the two notes resolves.

questions.topic: The final bar line against the double bar line
questions.learningObjective: tell the bar line that ends a piece from the one that ends a section
questions.stem: A part in 4/4, common time, in g major ends its last section with a bar line whose left stroke is thin and whose right stroke is thick, and closes the movement with a bar line of two thin strokes joined thickly at the top and bottom. What does each of those two marks tell a reader?

options.text: The thin and thick pair marks the end of the movement, while the joined pair marks the end of a section that continues in another key
options.misconception: swaps the two marks

options.text: Both marks mean the same thing, since any bar line at the end of a written page ends the music
options.misconception: treats both marks as equivalent

options.text: The thin and thick pair marks the end of a section inside a movement, while the two thin strokes joined at top and bottom mark the end of the movement itself
The thin and thick pair is a repeat sign, and the joined pair is a double bar line, so the first replays the section and the second divides it
options.misconception: calls a double bar line a repeat sign

questions.explanation: Bar lines are graded by how much they close, and the grading runs from the thinnest division to the thickest ending. A single bar line divides a movement, a double bar line of two thin strokes divides it more firmly, a thin-and-thick pair marks the end of a section, and the final bar line, with its two strokes joined at the top and the bottom, marks the end of the movement. The practical value of the distinction is that a reader can tell at a glance whether there is more music to come, and that is why the final mark is drawn differently and cannot be confused with the others. The trap in the first option reverses the two, which is the natural mistake when both are being learned at once, and the third confuses a double bar line with a repeat sign, which is told by the dots and not by the thickness. The trap in the second is the belief that the page's end does the work of the notation, which in a part extracted from a score is exactly the case where the final bar line matters.
questions.hint: The thicker the ending, the more final it is, and only one of the two marks closes the movement.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that counts the bars of a repeated structure
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that returns the performed bar count of a repeat structure
questions.stem: Trace the rule played(section, times, ending), which returns the number of bars a structure sounds: played(section, times, ending) = return section * times + ending, where ending is the number of bars in a final ending played only on the last pass. Apply it to a repeated section of eight bars with times equal to 2 and a second ending of three bars, in 4/4, common time, in c major. What does the rule return?

options.text: Sixteen bars, since 8 times 2 is 16 and a second ending is part of the repeated section and so is already counted
options.misconception: double counts by ignoring the extra ending

options.text: Nineteen bars, since 8 times 2 is 16 and 16 plus the 3 bars of the second ending is 19
Twenty-two bars, since 8 times 2 is 16 and both the first and the second ending add three bars each
options.misconception: counts the first ending as well as the second

options.text: Eleven bars, since the section plays once and only the second ending is added, so 8 plus 3 is 11
options.misconception: ignores the repeat

questions.explanation: The rule is one multiplication and one addition, and the two operations correspond to the two things a repeat structure does. The multiplication counts the passes: a section of eight bars heard twice gives 8 times 2, which is 16. The addition then counts what is not part of the passes, and the only such thing is the second ending, because the repeat's forward sign covers the first eight bars and both endings sit outside it, with the first ending heard on the first pass and the second on the last. So the total is 16 plus 3, which is 19, and the cross-check is to add the bars by hand: eight for the first pass, the first ending's three for 11, then eight again for 19, then the second ending's three for 22, which is a different structure and shows why the two endings must not both be added. The trap in the second option is exactly that over-count, and the third is the reading in which the repeat is ignored. The trap in the first is the plausible assumption that the endings are inside the repeated span.
questions.hint: Multiply the section by the number of passes, then add the bars of the ending that is played once.

questions.topic: Ordering accidentals by how far they reach
questions.learningObjective: rank the scope of the different kinds of accidental
questions.stem: Four kinds of marking can change how a note is read in a part in 4/4, common time, in c major. The key signature covers a whole movement, an accidental covers a single bar, a courtesy accidental covers the single note it stands beside, and an 8va bracket covers every note beneath it. Put the four in order from the widest reach to the narrowest.

options.text: The key signature first, then the 8va bracket, then the accidental, then the courtesy accidental, because a signature governs the movement, a bracket governs a written span, an accidental governs a bar, and a courtesy sign governs one note
The accidental first, then the courtesy accidental, then the 8va bracket, then the key signature, since the most local instruction must be read first when the marks conflict
options.misconception: orders by reading order rather than by reach

options.text: The key signature first, then the accidental, then the courtesy accidental, then the 8va bracket, since a bracket is a dynamic shape and so reaches least far
options.misconception: reads a bracket as a local mark

options.text: The key signature and the 8va bracket together first, then the accidental and the courtesy accidental together, because the first pair are written at the start of the part and the second pair beside notes
options.misconception: groups by position on the page

questions.explanation: The criterion is how much of the music a mark governs, and the four sit at four different scales. A key signature is printed once at the start and fixes the normal state of every letter for the whole movement, which makes it the widest. An 8va bracket is printed over a span and applies to every note beneath it, which is narrower because the span is chosen by the composer. An accidental applies to one letter at one octave for the rest of its bar, and a courtesy accidental applies to the single note it stands beside, which makes it the narrowest. The reason the order matters practically is that a reader resolves conflicts from the widest inward: the signature sets the baseline, the bracket shifts the register, the accidental adjusts one letter, and the courtesy sign confirms one note, and a later and narrower mark overrides a wider one. The trap in the first option is reading order, which is a plausible heuristic that fails here because an accidental printed early in a bar can still override a signature, and the third groups by typography rather than by reach.
questions.hint: Sort by how much of the music each marking governs, from the whole movement down to a single note.

questions.topic: The three positions of a snare drum note
questions.learningObjective: name the three notated positions of a snare drum note
questions.stem: A drum part in 4/4, common time, in c major is written on a one-line percussion staff, and three written notes appear on that single line with stems pointing three different ways. What are the three drum surfaces those three positions name, and what does the single line mean?

options.text: They are the bass drum, the snare drum and the cymbal, and the single line means the part is pitched an octave below the other staves
options.misconception: gives an octave transposition to a one-line percussion staff

options.text: They are the snare drum, the hi-hat and the ride cymbal, and the single line means the three are the same drum written three ways
options.misconception: confuses drums with cymbals

options.text: They are three different octaves of the snare drum, and the single line is a treble staff with one line left visible
options.misconception: treats a one-line staff as a truncated pitched staff

options.text: They are the snare drum, the middle tom and the floor tom, and the single line stands for the drum rather than for a pitch, which is why those notes carry no octave and no accidental

questions.explanation: Percussion notation uses staff position to name a drum rather than a pitch, and the standard one-line staff has three positions that matter, with the middle of the line for the snare drum and the spaces above and below it for the two toms. A note written on a percussion staff therefore has no octave, and an accidental beside it would be unusual, because the sign is the drum's name rather than a pitch. The single line is not a shortened pitched staff, which is the trap in the third option, and a percussion staff is never transposed by the octave convention that a double bass uses, which rules out the first. Cymbals are notated on a different set of positions, above the drum line and with their own shapes, and that is what the second option confuses. The reason the convention is worth knowing is that a player reading a part has to know the surface before the rhythm, since the same written line with two different surfaces is a different piece of music.
questions.hint: On a one-line percussion staff the position names the drum, not a pitch.

questions.topic: A cue note and how a player reads it
questions.learningObjective: say what a cue note is for and how it differs from the part itself
questions.stem: An orchestral score in 4/4, common time, in c major prints a short run of small notes above the top of the oboe's staff, headed by a small cue mark, and the oboe's own notes are absent for those bars. What is the small run, and what does it tell the oboist to do?

options.text: The small run is an ossia, a simplified alternative version of the oboe's own line that the player may use in place of the printed music
options.misconception: calls a cue an ossia

options.text: The small run is a rehearsal mark showing where the oboe enters, and it tells the player to wait until that point before beginning
options.misconception: reads a cue as an entry point

options.text: The small run is a cue, a short quotation of another player's line that the oboist is to play, and it tells the oboist to supply the notes the score has left out of their own staff
The small run is the oboe's line printed small for economy of space, and the oboist plays it exactly as it appears at written pitch
options.misconception: treats a cue as a reduction of the same line

questions.explanation: A cue exists because a score's staves can each be too busy to show everything that has to be played, and a cue solves that by printing a short quotation of the relevant line in small notes above the staff that needs it. The player whose staff is missing the notes plays the cue instead, at the pitch the small notes show, and the two are the same music even though they are written differently. That last point is what separates a cue from an ossia, since an ossia is an alternative version of the player's own line that changes the music while a cue reproduces another player's line unchanged. A cue is also a practical aid in rehearsal and in performance, since it tells a player not only what to play but who is playing it with them. The trap in the second option confuses a cue with a rehearsal letter or an entry point, and the third misreads the small size as a reduction, when in fact the size signals that the notes belong to somebody else.
questions.hint: A cue quotes another player line in small notes so that the player with the incomplete staff can still play.

questions.topic: Reading a table of bar line marks
questions.learningObjective: extract from a table what each bar line mark ends
questions.stem: A table of notation marks in 4/4, common time, in c major lists six rows: a single thin bar line, which divides a movement; a double bar line of two thin strokes, which divides it more firmly; a thin and thick pair, which ends a section; a final bar line joined at the top and bottom, which ends the movement; a backward repeat sign with dots, which sends the player back; and a forward repeat sign with dots, which marks where the return lands. Which two rows together mean that a span of music is performed twice?

options.text: The double bar line and the thin and thick pair, since two divisions in a row always indicate that the enclosed music is repeated
options.misconception: treats a division as a repetition

options.text: The backward repeat sign and the forward repeat sign, since the backward sign sends the player back and the forward sign marks the bar the return lands on, and a span needs both to be repeated
The backward repeat sign and the final bar line, since a repeat sign sends the player back and the final bar line closes the return at the end of the movement
options.misconception: pairs the repeat with the final bar line

options.text: The forward repeat sign and the single thin bar line, since a forward repeat must be followed by an ordinary bar line to take effect
options.misconception: believes a plain bar line activates a repeat

questions.explanation: The table separates three different jobs, and only two of the six rows belong to the same job. A division of any kind, whether a single line, a double line or a thin and thick pair, tells the reader where one stretch of music ends and another begins, and none of them causes anything to be performed again. A repeat needs a matched pair, and the two halves do different work: the backward sign is the instruction, printed at the point the player must return from, and the forward sign is the destination, printed at the bar the return lands on. With both present the enclosed span sounds twice. The trap in the first option is the natural confusion between ending a section and repeating one, and the second pairs the instruction with the wrong destination, since the final bar line closes the movement and sends nobody anywhere. The trap in the third invents a dependency that does not exist, since a forward repeat sign works with the backward sign and not with a plain bar line.
questions.hint: Separation marks and repetition marks are different jobs, and a repetition needs an instruction and a destination.

questions.topic: A score written at concert pitch for a transposing part
questions.learningObjective: convert a score pitch to the written pitch a transposing part needs
questions.stem: A score in 4/4, common time, in f major prints a written sounding C5 in the horn staff's place, and the player reads a transposing part in which every written note sounds a perfect fifth below what is printed. What does the player read so that the sounding pitch is C5, and why must the two notations be kept apart?

options.text: The player reads a written G5, because a horn in F sounds a perfect fifth below its part, and the two notations are kept apart because a printed score and a player's part are different documents serving different readers
The player reads a written F5, because a perfect fifth below the written F5 is the sounding C5 and a fifth above C5 is F5
options.misconception: puts the transposition on the wrong side

options.text: The player reads a written C5 unchanged, because a score already prints every part at the pitch that part is notated
options.misconception: assumes a score prints transposing parts at their written pitch

options.text: The player reads a written C4, because a horn in F sounds a perfect fifth below its part and a perfect fifth below the written C4 is the sounding F3
options.misconception: moves the written note an octave too low

questions.explanation: A printed score and a player's part differ in one systematic way, and the difference is that a score shows sounding pitches for every staff while a transposing part shows written pitches for one player. The conversion is therefore a single shift, and its direction comes from the instrument: a horn in F sounds a perfect fifth below what it reads, so to obtain a sounding C5 the part must show the note a fifth above, which is G5. Keeping the two apart is what allows a score to be readable by a conductor, who needs to see the actual music, while a player reads a part that is transposed into a comfortable register. The trap in the first option applies the shift the wrong way, and the second denies the convention that makes transposing parts exist. The trap in the third is the useful near-miss, because it is right about the direction of the transposition and wrong about which note was given, and it shows how easily an octave error attaches to a fifth.
questions.hint: The part shows the note a perfect fifth above the sounding pitch, because a horn in F sounds a fifth below its part.

questions.topic: A claim about a bar line that the mark contradicts
questions.learningObjective: test a claim about notation against the mark that is printed
questions.stem: A copyist claims that a movement in 4/4, common time, in c major is printed throughout with a double bar line, so that every section division is doubled, and points to the last bar of the movement, which is joined at the top and the bottom. Is the claim right, and what does the last bar line show?

options.text: The claim is right, because a final bar line is simply the strongest form of a double bar line and the two are the same mark drawn more boldly
options.misconception: treats the final bar line as a heavy double bar line

options.text: The claim is false, because a final bar line is a repeat sign with the dots omitted, and it shows that the section is to be played again
options.misconception: reads a final bar line as a repeat

options.text: The claim is false, and the last bar line shows only that the page is full, since a part is a document rather than a piece of music
options.misconception: denies that the notation describes the music

options.text: The claim is false, because a bar line joined at the top and the bottom is the final bar line and it is a different mark from a double bar line, and it shows that the movement ends there rather than dividing into sections

questions.explanation: The claim is a claim about notation, and notation can be checked directly, which is the point of testing it against the printed mark. A double bar line is two thin strokes side by side and it divides a movement, while the final bar line is two thin strokes joined at the top and the bottom, which is a different shape with a different job: it says the music stops. The last bar line of a part therefore proves that the movement ends at that point, and it also disproves the copyist's claim, since a joined pair is not a doubled line. The trap in the first option is the tempting identification of the two marks by their similar ingredients, and it is worth noticing that a composer who wants a very strong division does sometimes use a thick-and-thin pair at a key change, so the visual family is crowded and the exact shape matters. The trap in the second invents a repeat, and the third denies the connection between the notation and the music that is the whole premise of reading a part.
questions.hint: A double bar line is two separate strokes, and the final bar line is two strokes joined at the top and bottom.

questions.topic: Tracing a rule that respells a note enharmonically
questions.learningObjective: trace a rule that converts a spelled pitch to its enharmonic name
questions.stem: Trace the rule enharmonic(w), which returns the same sounding pitch under the next letter name: enharmonic(w) = return the next letter above the letter of w, with whatever accidental makes that letter sound at the pitch of w. Apply it to a written B4, a written E4, a written F sharp 4 and a written B sharp 4, all in 4/4, common time, in c major. What four names does the rule return?

options.text: The rule returns C5, F4, G4 and C5, because the next letter is taken with no accidental, on the ground that the pitch is already the next letter's natural
options.misconception: adds no accidental at all

options.text: The rule returns C6, Fb5, Gb5 and C6, because the rule always raises the octave, so the returned note lies an octave above the pitch it replaces
options.misconception: raises the octave regardless of the pitch

options.text: C flat 5, F flat 4, G flat 4 and C5, since each result keeps the pitch and takes the next letter, so B4 becomes C flat 5, E4 becomes F flat 4, F sharp 4 becomes G flat 4 and B sharp 4 needs no accidental at all
The rule returns B4, E4, F sharp 4 and B sharp 4 unchanged, because a note's name and its letter are independent, so a rule may change the letter or the sound but not both
options.misconception: believes the rule must change one or the other

questions.explanation: The rule has two jobs and the accidental is the part that needs arithmetic. The letter becomes the next one in the alphabet, and the accidental becomes whatever makes that new letter sound at the pitch that was already required, which is a statement about sound and not about notation. For B4 the next letter is C, and the B natural already sounds as the C flat below C5, so the answer is C flat 5. For E4 the next letter is F, and the E natural sounds as the F flat below F4, so the answer is F flat 4. For F sharp 4 the next letter is G, and the F sharp sounds as the G flat below G4, so the answer is G flat 4. The fourth case is the one that shows the rule has no built-in accidental: B sharp 4 already sounds as the C natural, and the next letter is C, so no accidental is needed and the answer is a plain C5. The octave follows from the sound in every case, which is why the second option's blanket octave shift is wrong. The first option adds no accidental at all and so returns the wrong pitch three times out of four, and the second denies that the accidental is derived from the pitch at all.
questions.hint: Take the next letter, then ask which accidental on that letter produces the pitch you already had.

questions.topic: Reading a table of accidentals against their scope
questions.learningObjective: read from a table which pitch each kind of accidental produces
questions.stem: A table of accidentals in 4/4, common time, in c major gives four rows. Row one: a sharp on the letter C, which sounds C sharp 4. Row two: a flat on the letter E, which sounds E flat 4. Row three: a double sharp on the letter F, which sounds F double sharp 4. Row four: a double flat on the letter B, which sounds B double flat 4. Which two rows give a pitch a semitone above the letter's own place in c major, and what are those two pitches?

options.text: Rows two and four, and the pitches are D4 and C4, since a flat and a double flat each raise the note to the next letter of the scale
options.misconception: turns a lowering accidental into a raising one

options.text: Rows one and three, and the pitches are C sharp 4 and G4, since a sharp raises its letter by a semitone and a double sharp by two, while a flat lowers its letter by a semitone and a double flat by two
Rows one and two, and the pitches are C sharp 4 and D4, since a sharp raises a letter and a flat also raises it to the next diatonic degree
options.misconception: claims a flat raises its letter

options.text: Rows one and three give the two highest pitches of the four, and their names are C double sharp 4 and G sharp 4, since a double sharp is two sharps
options.misconception: names a double sharp as a double-sharpened letter

questions.explanation: Each accidental moves its letter by a fixed amount in a fixed direction, and the four rows are built to make that a single comparison. A sharp raises its letter by a semitone, so the C becomes C sharp; a double sharp raises it by two semitones, so the F, which in c major sounds as F natural, becomes F sharp and so is named F double sharp; a flat lowers its letter by a semitone, so the E becomes E flat; and a double flat lowers it by two semitones, so the B, which in c major sounds as B natural, becomes A and so is named B double flat. The two rows that raise their letter are therefore the first and the third, and each produces a pitch above its letter's natural one, which for the C is C sharp 4 and for the F is G4. That the double sharp lands on a different letter name from the letter it is written on is the feature worth noticing, and it is what the third option stumbles over. The trap in the first option reverses the direction of a flat, and the second claims a flat raises its letter.
questions.hint: A sharp raises its letter by a semitone, a flat lowers it by a semitone, and a double accidental does twice as much.
